sens: bright and sudden light that flashes from the sky during a storm
intense and brief glow that shines and disappears
ray that splits the sky in a zigzag pattern
shining point of an arrow or weapon
divine manifestation accompanied by fire and light
H1300B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the bright and instantaneous light produced by a storm: it is a natural phenomenon that everyone has seen. In Exodus 19:16, during the giving of the Law at Sinai, Moses reports that "thunderings, lightnings, and a thick cloud" appear on the mountain: this is the image of God's power manifesting with force.
2. The word can also simply refer to a sudden and intense brightness, a sparkle: Job 20:25 speaks of an arrow that "flashes" as it emerges from the body — the image is that of an object shining brightly and briefly.
3. Lightning becomes an image of swift speed and destructive power. In Psalms 144:6, the psalmist asks God to "flash the lightning" to scatter his enemies: this is asking God to act with the force and suddenness of lightning.
4. Figuratively, lightning represents the sharp and shining point of a weapon: in Ezekiel 21:33, the sword of judgment "flashes" — it shines with fearsome effectiveness.
5. In prophetic visions, lightning appears as a sign of divine presence and power. In Ezekiel 1:13, the heavenly creatures surrounded by fire emit "lightnings": this is the superhuman, luminous, and terrifying atmosphere of God's presence.
H1300B.origine: The Hebrew word baraq comes from a root that evokes the idea of something that shines, sparkles, or suddenly bursts forth. The root is also the source of names: Barak, the military leader of Israel during the time of the Judges, bears this name which means "the lightning" — a symbol of speed and warrior power. In the daily life of the Middle East, lightning is a spectacular and feared phenomenon, which explains why it spontaneously becomes an image of divine power and sudden action.
H1300B.emploi: The word lightning appears about 21 times in the Old Testament, mostly in descriptions of divine manifestations and in the psalms of praise. It is particularly frequent in the writings of the prophets Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Zechariah, who use it to describe God's glory, His judgment, or His warrior action. In the Psalms, lightning illustrates both God's protective power (Psalms 77:19: "The lightnings lit up the world") and His ability to scatter enemies (Psalms 144:6). In Job, the word also refers to the brightness of a weapon. The image is almost always associated with a spectacular, swift, and overwhelming divine manifestation: it conveys the idea of an irresistible and superhuman action.
H1300B.portee: For the biblical reader, lightning is much more than a meteorological phenomenon: it is the vivid image of God's power acting in history. When the Bible speaks of lightnings, it invites the believer to recognize that God is not distant or silent, but present, visible, and active with superhuman strength. This image reassures the persecuted or anxious believer: God can intervene as suddenly and powerfully as lightning to defend him.

sens: Warrior and judge of Israel during the time of the Judges
Son of Abinoam of Kedesh-Naphtali
Deliverer of Israel from the yoke of Jabin and Sisera
H1301.detail: 1. Barak is a military leader of Israel who lived during the time of the Judges, before the monarchy. His name literally means "lightning" or "flash of lightning," which evokes his speed and power in battle. Deborah, a prophetess from Ephraim, calls him to lead Israel against the oppressive Canaanites (Judges 4:6). 2. He is the son of Abinoam and resides in Kedesh-Naphtali, a city in northern Israel. Deborah commands him to go to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun to confront Sisera, the enemy general (Judges 4:6-10). 3. Barak becomes the deliverer of Israel: the Lord routes Sisera's army before him, destroying the chariots and scattering the enemy camp (Judges 4:15). Although Barak pursues Sisera, it is ultimately a woman, Jael, who kills the fugitive, which Deborah had predicted by saying that the glory of this victory would not go to Barak (Judges 4:9, 22). 4. Barak celebrates this victory in a song with Deborah, calling for praise to the Lord for this deliverance (Judges 5:1, 12).
H1301.origine: The name Barak means "lightning" or "flash of lightning" in Hebrew, an image that suits a warrior known for his strength and swiftness. It is a meaningful name, typical of the biblical era, characterizing the one who bears it. Barak belongs to the ancient history of Israel, before the people had kings.
H1301.emploi: Barak is mentioned thirteen times in the Bible, all in the Book of Judges, mainly in chapters 4 and 5. In chapter 4, the account recounts how Deborah summons him to lead Israel into battle against Sisera, general of Jabin, king of Canaan. Barak agrees on the condition that Deborah accompanies him (Judges 4:8). He gathers ten thousand men and leads them into battle (Judges 4:10). The Lord grants victory, Sisera flees, and Barak pursues him (Judges 4:15-16, 22). In chapter 5, Barak and Deborah sing together their victory and celebrate God's intervention (Judges 5:1, 12, 15). Barak's role shows a leader quick to obey God's word through a prophetess, but also aware of his insufficiency without divine presence.
H1301.portee: The story of Barak teaches the Christian reader that true victory comes from God, not from human strength, even that of a great warrior. Barak recognizes his need to be accompanied by Deborah, the prophetess, which symbolizes the importance of listening to God's word. His life shows that a faithful leader must be humble before God and willing to receive His orders through whatever instrument He chooses, without concern for personal honor. He is a model of faith and obedience.

sens: ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile
H1302.detail: Barkos is the name of a family leader among the temple servants ("Nethinim") who left the Babylonian captivity to return to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. His name appears in both lists of return from exile, first in Ezra 2:53, then repeated in Nehemiah 7:55, always among the families of sanctuary servants. His descendants bear his name and form a recognized house of the restored people.
H1302.origine: The name Barkos literally means "the cut-off son" in Hebrew (from bar, "son," and qos, which evokes a cut or separation). This meaning may highlight a significant origin or separation in the history of this family, although the exact context eludes us. The name reflects a common practice among the Hebrews: naming children based on significant events or circumstances.
H1302.emploi: Barkos appears only twice in the Bible, in the two places where the families of temple servants returned from Babylon are listed. The passage in Ezra 2 and its parallel in Nehemiah 7 maintain the same list, confirming Barkos's importance as the founder of a lineage of temple servants established in Jerusalem after 538 B.C. It is one of the many families of Nethinim who formed a class of sacred workers attached to the temple worship.

sens: Spiny desert plant with sharp prickles
Instrument of punishment using these thorns
H1303.detail:
1. The thistle is a wild plant that grows in arid regions, covered with sharp prickles. Gideon refers to it as thorns of the desert to punish the elders of Succoth (Judges 8:7, 8:16), as their thorns caused intense pain.
2. Used as a means of punishment, the thistle becomes an instrument of torture. Although the Bible does not detail exactly how this punishment was inflicted, the image is one of suffering inflicted by these sharp prickles of desert plants.
H1303.origine: The Hebrew word barqanim comes from a root that evokes the idea of piercing or tearing. These thorny plants are native to the arid lands of the Middle East, where they pose a constant problem for inhabitants and livestock. The term applies to various kinds of thorns and thistles that cover the desert landscape.
H1303.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in the two verses reporting the incident at Succoth. Gideon, returning victorious from his battle against the Midianites, comes to ask the elders of the city for food, which they refuse him. In response, he punishes these elders by torturing them with thistles from the desert. This punishment was a severe form of physical punishment, reserved for those who had failed in their duty of hospitality and shown their disbelief in the victory promised by the Lord.
H1303.portee: This passage shows us the severity of divine judgment on disbelief and refusal to obey. The thistle, a symbol of pain and punishment, reminds us that doubt towards God's promises has tangible consequences. For the Christian, this invites trust and obedience, rather than rebellion which brings suffering.

sens: Precious green stone
Element of the high priest's breastplate in Israel's worship
H1304A.detail:
1. The emerald is a precious green stone, highly valued in antiquity for its beauty and rarity. It is a hard and brilliant gem that ranked among the most precious riches of ancient kingdoms.
2. In Israel's worship, the emerald held a special place: it was the first element of the first row of the twelve stones set in the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17 and 39:10). This stone symbolized the presence of God in the sanctuary and the excellence of the worship rendered to the Lord.
H1304A.origine: The Hebrew word בָּרֶקֶת comes from a root that denotes brightness and brilliance. It is a stone known in Mesopotamia and Egypt under similar names. The Bible uses this term to refer to this precious green gem, integrated into the context of temple worship as a symbol of beauty and holiness.
H1304A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the context of the high priest's breastplate. Exodus 28:17 and 39:10 describe the adornment of four rows of precious stones on the breastplate, with the emerald listed first in the first row. These two passages repeat the same text, likely in different narrative contexts (the divine plan and its realization).
H1304A.portee: The emerald reminds the people of Israel that worship rendered to God must embody beauty, purity, and preciousness. This stone, among the most beautiful created, symbolizes how serving the Lord requires the best and noblest. It invites us to honor God not out of routine, but with reverence and magnificence of heart.

sens: Green precious stone, variety of beryl
Gem of great value, royal or divine ornament
H1304B.detail:
1. The emerald is a precious green stone, varying in its tones according to its purity. In the Bible, it ranks among the most precious stones known and worked by ancient Egypt and the Near East.
2. The Bible mentions the emerald as a high-value ornament, symbolizing splendor and wealth. In Ezekiel 28:13, it lists the stones that adorned the king of Tyre in his original majesty, showing that the emerald was a royal jewel and a sign of divine glory.
H1304B.origine: The Hebrew word barqat (בָּֽרְקַת) designates a precious stone whose name may be linked to brightness or brilliance. It is a variant of the word bareqet (בָּרֶ֫קֶת), both relating to brilliant and precious stones. The Greek word anthrax or smaragdos translates this concept in the Septuagint and refers to the gem that captivated the admiration of the ancients.
H1304B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 28:13, where the prophet lists the precious stones that adorned the king of Tyre in his state of original glory. This passage describes the paradisiacal splendor of the sovereign before his fall, placing the emerald alongside other jewels like sardius, topaz, sapphire, and jasper. This enumeration highlights the brilliance and wealth that characterized this king before his pride.
H1304B.portee: The emerald reminds the believer that beauty and material wealth, no matter how precious, do not guarantee spiritual stability. The fall of the king of Tyre, despite the splendor of his ornaments, invites us to seek true wealth not in temporal goods but in wisdom and obedience to God. This precious stone thus becomes a symbol of the vanity of earthly glories.

sens: Make pure, clean by removing what soils
Choose among others, select what is excellent
Make bright, polish, sharpen
Test, put to the test to verify quality
H1305.detail:
1. To make pure means to eliminate impurities, to clean completely. It is an act of physical or moral purification: "you show yourself pure" with one who is pure (Psalms 18:27) means that a righteous person reveals their purity in front of another righteous person.
2. To choose or select is to retain what is best among several: the "chosen" sheep prepared in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 5:18) are the finest, the best of the flock, sorted from the others.
3. To polish or make bright applies to what one wants to make shine: a "sharp" arrow (Isaiah 49:2) is a refined and polished arrow to be formidable, or a purified tongue to speak clearly (Zephaniah 3:9).
4. To test or try means to submit to a trial to recognize true value: the righteous are "chosen" and refined in the trial (Daniel 12:10) as fire purifies gold.
H1305.origine: The Hebrew verb barar comes from a root that evokes the action of separating, sifting, making clear and distinct. It is related to words meaning "bright" and "clear." This root conveys the idea of distinction and separation: separating the pure from the impure, the good from the bad, what shines from what is dull. The word suggests an active and voluntary action to achieve clarity and purity.
H1305.emploi: This verb appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic books. It carries several nuances: it can describe the action of purifying oneself or being purified ("purify yourselves" in Isaiah 52:11), that of choosing the best among a group (the chosen sheep, the chosen gatekeepers), that of refining and polishing what one prepares (sharp arrows), or that of testing someone through adversity (Daniel 12:10: "many will be purified, made white, and tested"). The context changes the nuance of the word, but the central idea remains: to separate and make distinct what is excellent or pure.
H1305.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that purity is not innate but acquired through an active process: it requires purifying oneself, choosing the good, allowing God to test us to refine our faith like gold in the fire. It also reveals that God recognizes and cherishes those who are pure in heart, and that He goes through difficulties with us to purify and prepare us.

sens: King of Gomorrah during the time of the patriarchs
H1306.detail: Birscha is the king of Gomorrah mentioned only once in the Bible, during the account of war between the kings of the Jordan Valley. He is cited in Genesis 14:2 alongside the kings of Sodom, Admah, and Zeboiim, as one of the rulers who rebelled against Kedorlaomer and his allies.
H1306.origine: The name Birscha literally means "with iniquity" or "with wickedness" in Hebrew (bir = "with" and scha = "wickedness"). Although we know nothing else about this king, the meaning of his name evokes malice — which may reflect the moral reputation of Gomorrah in biblical tradition.
H1306.emploi: Birscha appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 14:2. He is presented as one of the five kings of the Jordan Valley who unite to wage war against Kedorlaomer. This event is set against the historical backdrop of wars between peoples during the time of Abraham. After this mention, Birscha completely disappears from the biblical narrative.

sens: City of Benjamin mentioned as the homeland of a warrior of David
H1307.detail: Béroth is a locality whose name means "the wells" in Hebrew. One of David's warriors, Nahraï, is from there (1 Chronicles 11:39).
H1307.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew "berot" (בְּאֵרוֹת), which means "wells" in the plural. It is a city in the Benjamin region, likely named for the water wells that marked the site.
H1307.emploi: Béroth appears only once in the provided texts, in 1 Chronicles 11:39, where it is the birthplace of Nahraï, one of the warriors in King David's elite guard and bearer of Joab's weapons.

sens: Watercourse in southern Judah
Dry streambed or wadi
H1308.detail:
1. Besor is a watercourse located at the extreme south of the kingdom of Judah, near Philistine lands, and flows into the Mediterranean Sea. It is a real geographical location that David and his men encounter during their pursuit of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:9).
2. The name evokes a torrent or a streambed that can be dry depending on the seasons — in Hebrew, this type of watercourse is called a wadi. Two hundred of David's six hundred men declare themselves too tired to cross this Besor, showing that it represents a real physical obstacle (1 Samuel 30:10).
H1308.origine: The name "Besor" literally means "joyful" or "cheerful" in Hebrew, although the watercourse bears this name as an established geographical designation. No etymological link explains here the original meaning of the name applied to this southern wadi; it is simply the traditional name of the place since antiquity.
H1308.emploi: Besor appears three times in the Bible, all in the same account: 1 Samuel 30, when David pursues the Amalekites who plundered Ziklag. First, David reaches the Besor with six hundred men (1 Samuel 30:9); then, two hundred men stop there, too tired to continue (1 Samuel 30:10); finally, David finds these two hundred men at the Besor upon his return and welcomes them kindly (1 Samuel 30:21). This watercourse serves as a geographical landmark and a point of division in the narrative of this military campaign.
H1308.portee: This account of the Besor shows how David, despite his impatience to recover the captives and the plunder taken by the Amalekites, treats with respect those who cannot follow him. He recognizes the importance of those who guard the baggage — a teaching on the value of each person in the community, regardless of their warrior contribution. The Besor thus becomes a witness to a justice and kindness that characterize the true leader in the eyes of God.

sens: happy information, joyful news
announcement of a favorable event
message brought by a messenger
reward given to the bearer of good news
H1309.detail:
1. The good news is primarily happy information, news that delights the recipient. In 2 Kings 7:9, the lepers speak of "a day of good news" upon discovering that the Syrian army has lifted the siege: it is the announcement of deliverance.
2. The word also refers to the message itself, what is reported by the messenger. In 2 Samuel 18:25, the king watches for the one who arrives and says: "If he is alone, he brings news" — the runner carries an important message.
3. By extension, it is the reward or payment given to the one who brings the good news. In 2 Samuel 4:10, the king declares that he should give a "reward" to the one who would announce Saul's death — but he has him killed instead of rewarding him, because this false news disappoints him.
H1309.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to bear" or "to bring," with the sense of "bringing good news." The same root is found in other Hebrew words denoting announcement and message. The initial image is that of the messenger running with his information: he bears the news as one bears a precious object.
H1309.emploi: The word appears 6 times in biblical Hebrew, almost exclusively in the accounts of 2 Samuel and 2 Kings. It is mainly used when a runner or messenger arrives to announce an important event — the death of a king, the lifting of a siege. The context is always that of awaited information that calms or delights the king and his close ones. In 2 Samuel 18:20 and 18:27, Joab initially refuses Achimaats the right to run, then the king recognizes in him "a good man" who brings good news: the word values the messenger who brings hope.
H1309.portee: This notion of good news reminds us that God loves to communicate with His people, and that the announcement of His deliverance, victory, or grace transforms the heart of the one who receives it. It is on this image that the authors of the New Testament build the word gospel (euangelion in Greek): the Good News of salvation in Jesus Christ is the message that must be carried to all men, just as the runner once carried the announcement of the king.

sens: To boil or cook food
To roast or prepare meat with heat
To let ripen or come to maturity
H1310.detail:
1. To boil or cook food with heat, in a pot or container: this is the basic preparation of food. The manna in the desert was prepared this way: the people "cooked it in a pot" to make cakes (Numbers 11:8).

2. To roast or prepare meat, especially during sacrifices or meals. In the temple, the priests "cooked" the meat of the sacrifices in a specially designated place (Ezekiel 46:20). It also means to cook over high heat: to roast rather than boil.

3. To come to maturity or to ripen fruits: the vine whose "blossom developed and its clusters gave ripe grapes" (Genesis 40:10) is a poetic image. The word can describe the natural process of ripening.
H1310.origine: The Hebrew root בשׁל describes the action of transforming food by heat or fruit by time. It is linked to the idea of completeness: something cooked is finished, ready. This root is found in several forms depending on the role of the subject: one can cook something (that is to cook), be cooked oneself (that is the undergone transformation), or bring something to cook (that is to lead to cooking).
H1310.emploi: The verb appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the accounts concerning food and sacrifices. It is particularly frequent in Exodus and Leviticus: God commands how to cook the Passover (Exodus 12:9), how to prepare the sacrifices (Exodus 29:31), how to treat the leftovers (Exodus 23:19). It is also found in difficult moments: in famine, it designates the unthinkable (2 Kings 6:29). The word can be literal (cooking meat) or figurative (ripening, maturity).
H1310.portee: This simple verb reminds us that the patient preparation of food is an ordinary and good act, inscribed in the created order. It invites us to respect the practical commandments of daily life and to recognize in the simple acts of cooking the order that God has placed in the world. When maturity is at stake, it speaks of patience and fulfillment.

sens: Prepared by the heat of fire, boiled or cooked in water
Prepared by cooking, as opposed to raw or roasted
H1311.detail:
1. The word describes meat or food prepared by heat, particularly by immersing it in boiling water. In Exodus 12:9, during the Passover meal, God commands that the Passover lamb not be eaten "cooked" in water, but roasted over fire: this prohibition shows that "cooked" specifically means boiled or cooked in water, as opposed to roasting.
2. More broadly, the word qualifies any food prepared by heat according to a given method. In Numbers 6:19, the "cooked" shoulder of the sacrificial ram is offered to the Nazarite after his vow: here, "cooked" simply refers to meat that is cooked, prepared, and edible, without specifying whether it is cooked in water or over fire.
H1311.origine: The Hebrew verb bâshel literally means "to cook," "to boil." The adjective "bashel" (בָּשֵׁל) is its participial or adjectival form: it describes the state of what has been cooked. The root evokes the action of subjecting something to heat and water to transform it and make it edible.
H1311.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to qualify meat or cooked food. In Exodus 12:9, it is used negatively: God refuses that the Passover lamb be "cooked" in water, for the Passover requires roasting over fire, which symbolizes a swift and direct deliverance. In Numbers 6:19, it positively describes the shoulder of the sacrificial ram, which must be cooked to be offered to the Nazarite. The context changes, but the meaning remains: food transformed by cooking.
H1311.portee: For the Christian reader, these two passages teach that the manner of preparing an offering or a sacred meal is important to God: it is not just about eating, but about following His precise instructions. The Passover roasted over fire recalls the urgency and power of deliverance, while the carefully prepared sacrifice shows the respect due to God in worship.

sens: Persian officer in Judea during the time of Ezra
H1312.detail: Bishlam is a Persian officer who lived in Judea during the return from exile, in the time of King Artaxerxes. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:7, where he is among those who wrote to the king of Persia to oppose the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. His name means "in peace" in Persian, reflecting the foreign origin of this character in the political context of restored Judea.
H1312.origine: The name Bishlam is of Persian origin and literally means "in peace" (from bis, "peace"). This name reflects the political and administrative environment of Achaemenid Persia, where officers often bore Persian proper names. Its appearance in the Aramaic text of Ezra 4 shows how Persian authorities intervened directly in the affairs of Judea during the return from exile.
H1312.emploi: Bishlam appears only once in Scripture, in Ezra 4:7. He is presented as one of the Persian officers who, alongside Mithredath and Thabeel, sent a letter to King Artaxerxes to contest the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem by the Judeans returned from exile. This letter was written in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian administration, and it testifies to the opposition that the Judeans faced in their efforts to restore their place of worship.

sens: Spice or fragrant substance used to perfume, season, or honor
Pleasant fragrance, sweet scent
H1313.detail:
1. The word designates a spice or a precious aromatic substance: myrrh, incense, balm, or other fragrant plants. In Song of Solomon 5:1, the beloved "gathers her myrrh with her aromatics," evoking these fragrant treasures harvested from Eastern gardens, both delicate and rich.
2. More broadly, it evokes the sweetness and pleasantness of the perfume itself: the agreeable smell that emanates from these substances. It is the image of what pleases the senses and touches the heart with its delicacy.
H1313.origine: The Hebrew word בֹּשֶׂם comes from a root that expresses the idea of sweetness and fragrance. It belongs to the family of words that describe pleasant scents and the substances that produce them — myrrh, incense, balm — all linked to ancient Eastern life, religious rituals, and moments of joy. These aromatics were precious, imported from distant regions.
H1313.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in common French (Segond translation). It is found in Song of Solomon 5:1, in a scene of intimacy and mutual delight: the beloved gathers her aromatics in her garden, a symbol of beauty, abundance, and shared pleasure. The context is that of the sensual and poetic celebration of love.
H1313.portee: The aromatics of the Song remind us that sensory beauty, fragrance, and sweetness are part of the life that God loves and blesses. Far from being condemned, the delicate and pure pleasures of love and joy are celebrated as precious gifts. This word invites the reader to see in beautiful and fragrant things an expression of divine abundance.

sens: Fragrant and precious substance derived from plants, used to perfume or sanctify
Spice or balm used in religious offering
Element of wealth and luxury, object of precious trade
Feeling or quality that spreads like a fragrance
H1314.detail:
1. An aromatic is a natural substance with a delicate fragrance, extracted from certain rare plants. The Bible distinguishes various kinds, often imported from distant lands: they are found with the Queen of Sheba, who brings them in great quantity to Solomon (1 Kings 10:2), testifying to their rarity and value.
2. God commands that aromatics be included in the sacred anointing oil (Exodus 25:6), making them materials of worship, intended to sanctify priests and temple objects. They are also burned as incense during religious services.
3. Kings boast of possessing aromatics among their riches (2 Chronicles 32:27), and they are offered as tribute or diplomatic gifts. They are a prestige good, a sign of power and refinement.
4. In the Song of Solomon, aromatics become a poetic image: the perfumes of the beloved surpass all aromatics in sweetness (4:10), and her garden is a bed of aromatics (6:2), evoking beauty that spreads and attracts.
H1314.origine: The Hebrew word בֶּשֶׂם (besem) literally means what exudes a smell, what smells good. It primarily designates the aromatic spices and balms that the ancient Near East exported from Southern Arabia and India. The Hebrew Bible uses it to name substances like myrrh, incense, spikenard, or other balsamic resins, all precious and costly. The word reflects the importance these products had in the commerce and religious life of the time.
H1314.emploi: The word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and poetic books. It concretely designates the spices and resins used in the temple (Exodus 25:6, 1 Chronicles 9:29): mixed with oil, they serve to anoint the king and the priests, marking the divine presence. The Song of Solomon uses it figuratively to express the sweetness and allure of the beloved, her invisible charm that spreads (4:10, 4:14). The kings of Israel and the powerful accumulate them as a sign of wealth and wisdom (1 Kings 10:2, 2 Chronicles 32:27). Isaiah also uses it in contrast: instead of perfume, vain women will wear a stench of decay (3:24), an image of God's judgment.
H1314.portee: Aromatics remind the believer that God invites His people to total consecration: these precious substances do not serve personal luxury, but the holiness of worship. Their rarity and cost teach that serving God deserves our most precious goods. In the Song, they symbolize how moral and spiritual beauty communicates subtly, attracting and blessing. For Christian life, they evoke the "fragrance" of Christ that believers spread around them (2 Corinthians 2:14-15).

sens: wife from the tribe of Judah during the united monarchy
H1315G.detail: Basmath is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when Israel was unified under the reign of Solomon. She is the daughter of Solomon and married Achimaaz, who was one of the officials responsible for the king's supply in the region of Naphtali (1 Kings 4:15). Thus, she was connected to Solomon's royal administration through her marriage to this high official.
H1315G.origine: The name Basmath means "spice" in Hebrew, evoking something fragrant, pleasant, and precious. This name likely reflects the esteem given to this woman of the royal court.
H1315G.emploi: Basmath appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:15. She is presented as the daughter of King Solomon, married to Achimaaz. This passage is part of an administrative list of the twelve commissioners that Solomon had established to govern the regions of Israel and provide for the needs of the king and his court. Basmath thus illustrates the marital alliances by which Solomon connected the great families to his central administration.

sens: Hittite woman, wife of Esau
daughter of Elon the Hittite
H1315H.detail: Basmath is a Hittite woman who becomes the wife of Esau. She appears in Genesis 26:34, where she is presented as the daughter of Elon, a Hittite, one of the two women that Esau takes at the age of forty. She is the mother of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn son.
H1315H.origine: The name Basmath means "spice" in Hebrew, evoking a precious and fragrant substance. It designates this woman from the generation of Isaac and Rebekah, during the time of the patriarchs.
H1315H.emploi: Basmath appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:34. She is mentioned as one of the two Hittite women that Esau marries, which contrasts with his mother Rebekah's plan for Jacob to marry a woman from his own family. Her role in the narrative is to show Esau's marital choices and illustrate the gap between the descendants of Abraham and the neighboring Canaanite peoples.

sens: Arab woman from the patriarchal era, daughter of Ishmael
Wife of Esau and mother of Reuel
H1315I.detail: Basmath is an Arab woman living during the time of the Patriarchs, the daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth, Kedar, and several other sons of Ishmael. She marries Esau, the son of Isaac, and becomes the mother of Reuel (Genesis 36:4). Her name means "spice," which was a precious commodity at that time. She appears in the genealogies of Esau, notably to mark the transmission of the family lineage through her son Reuel and his descendants (Genesis 36:10, 13, 17).
H1315I.origine: The Hebrew name בָּֽשְׂמַת (Basmath) literally means "spice" or "balm" (from the word שֹׂם which refers to precious aromatic substances). It is a name that reflects wealth and value in ancient Near Eastern culture.
H1315I.emploi: Basmath is mentioned five times in Genesis, all occurrences found in Genesis 36, the chapter that lists the genealogies and descendants of Esau. She is regularly identified as "Basmath, wife of Esau" and as the mother of Reuel (Genesis 36:3, 4, 10, 13, 17). These references show her role in establishing the Edomite lineages and her place in the patriarchal genealogies, although she is not the direct subject of narratives but rather an important figure for family continuity.

sens: Fertile region east of the Jordan, northeast of the Promised Land
Territory given to the half-tribe of Manasseh after the conquest
Land famous for its pastures and livestock
Region symbolizing divine fertility and prosperity
H1316.detail:
1. Bashan is a geographical region located east of the Jordan, in the ancient Levant. It extended northeast of the Promised Land and was known for its natural wealth. When the Israelites conquered this territory, Og, king of Bashan, came out to meet them to fight (Numbers 21:33).
2. After the victory over Og and his people, Moses assigned the territory of Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh, who established their dwellings there (Deuteronomy 3:13). This region thus became one of the portions of the Israelite territory in the Promised Land.
3. Bashan was renowned for its excellent pastures and prosperous livestock, particularly its high-quality cattle. The prophet Amos mentions the "cows of Bashan" to symbolize opulence and luxurious living (Amos 4:1).
4. In biblical language, Bashan represents abundance and divine blessing. The psalmist speaks of how the Lord will bring His people "from Bashan" (Psalms 68:23), using this fertile land as an image of restoration and protection.
H1316.origine: The name Bashan literally means "fruitful" in ancient Hebrew, revealing the biblical perception of this region as eminently productive and blessed. This fertility was due to the favorable climate, rich soils, and abundant water in this volcanic region of the Levant. The name reflects the deep impression this land of exceptional agricultural and pastoral prosperity made on its ancient inhabitants.
H1316.emploi: Bashan appears 53 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Chronicles) and the psalms. It is first mentioned during the conquest when Og, the last king of the Rephaim, governs this territory and confronts the Israelites (Numbers 21:33). After his defeat, Bashan becomes a permanent possession of Manasseh. The region then appears in lists of Levitical cities and in enumerations of districts of the kingdom of Israel. The prophets cite it as an example of prosperity (Isaiah 2:13 speaks of its cedars), and the psalms invoke it as a symbol of strength and divine blessing.
H1316.portee: Bashan reminds believers that God's promise includes material abundance and prosperity when the people remain in obedience. It is a concrete example of how God generously provides for those He calls, not only spiritually but also materially. This fertile region, given to Manasseh, also illustrates God's faithfulness in keeping His promises of inheritance and blessing through generations.

sens: State of trouble, humiliation, and moral disorder
Feeling of being covered with shame before others
Loss of dignity and assurance caused by dishonor
H1317.detail:
1. Confusion is primarily the state of disorder and disturbance experienced by one who is unmasked or defeated. In Hosea 10:6, "confusion will seize Ephraim" when the kingdom of Israel is delivered to Assyria: it is the turmoil, the dread that seizes a people confronted with their defeat and helplessness.
2. It is also the moral humiliation felt by one who has lost their dignity or honor. The word evokes the burning shame of being exposed in public, being judged, discovered. When it is read that Israel "will be ashamed of its plans" (Hosea 10:6), it is seen that confusion accompanies the awareness of its guilt.
H1317.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of loss of composure and dignity. It belongs to the family of terms that describe the opposite of honor: while honor pertains to what is hidden or preserved, confusion reveals and exposes. It is the absolute opposite of glory or prestige that one can maintain in honor.
H1317.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 10:6. In this context of divine judgment on the northern kingdom, confusion is the announced punishment: it accompanies Assyrian captivity. It is a direct consequence of Israel's unfaithfulness. The prophet uses this term to describe the internal collapse (humiliation) that will accompany the external collapse (military conquest). Confusion is not merely an emotional reaction but the result of divine judgment.
H1317.portee: Confusion is presented in this passage as the inevitable result of distancing from God. It reminds us that sin leads not only to material and social consequences but also to a profound loss of spiritual dignity. For the believer, this word invites an understanding that fleeing from God only leads to the crumbling of what truly constitutes us — our honor in Him.

sens: To walk on something or someone with force, to crush underfoot
To oppress, humiliate, treat with contempt
H1318.detail:
1. To tread means to walk on something or someone with force, crushing it underfoot. It is a physical action of trampling. In Amos 5:11, the prophet reproaches the rich for having "tread upon the poor": they have crushed him, dominated him, treated him brutally, as one treads underfoot what does not deserve respect.
2. By extension, to tread upon someone means to oppress, humiliate, reduce to powerlessness — to treat as something worthless. It is the image of a powerful man crushing the weak under his authority or contempt.
H1318.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּשַׁס (bashas) expresses the idea of trampling, of walking brutally on something. The root evokes a violent and contemptuous action: to tread underfoot. This verb is rare in the Bible, which underscores its expressive force when used.
H1318.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 5:11. The prophet Amos places it at the heart of an accusation against the rich who exploit the poor. By treading upon the poor — crushing him to extort grain — they have unjustly enriched themselves by building houses and planting vineyards. But their prosperity will be in vain: the prophet announces that they will not enjoy these goods. The verb thus summarizes all the social violence that Amos denounces.
H1318.portee: This word challenges the Christian on how he treats the weak and the poor. Treading upon the poor is a serious sin in the eyes of God: it is abuse of power, injustice, contempt for human dignity. Amos's condemnation reminds us that God sees and judges those who crush the little ones, and that ill-gotten wealth brings no true satisfaction.

sens: To bring, convey news, a message
To communicate joyful news, good tidings
To publish, proclaim news to the crowd
To announce, preach good news with divine authority
H1319.detail:
1. The verb primarily means simply to bring or convey news to someone: the messenger "brought the news" of Israel's defeat to Eli (1 Samuel 4:17), or "brings news" of the battle to David (2 Samuel 18:26). It is information communicated from one point to another.

2. When the news is joyful, the verb takes on a tone of gladness: to announce a victory as a "good news" (2 Samuel 4:10, 1 Chronicles 10:9). The messenger becomes a bearer of joy.

3. To publish or proclaim means to shout the news to many: "I proclaim your deliverance aloud" (Psalms 40:10), "Sing to the Lord a new song... publish his wonders" (Psalms 96:2). The news spreads through public announcement.

4. In a spiritual sense, it is to announce God's salvation: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news?" (Isaiah 41:27), "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor" (Isaiah 61:1). It is to proclaim divine grace.
H1319.origine: The Hebrew verb בשׂר (ba.sar) comes from the root בשׂר which essentially means "to bear news." The noun בשׂורה (be.sou.rah) means "good news" or "joyful announcement." The root evokes the concrete action of the messenger who runs to carry information from one place to another. In Greek, the New Testament will take up this notion in the gospel (euaggelion) and the action of evangelizing (euaggelizo), which directly translate this biblical idea of announcing the good news of salvation.
H1319.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical and prophetic books. In ancient times, it designates the messenger who runs to announce to David the news of the battle (2 Samuel 18:19-31), sometimes good news (victory), sometimes bad (death of Saul). The Psalms use it to celebrate: "I proclaim your righteousness" (Psalms 40:10), "Publish his wonders" (Psalms 96:2), where the believer becomes a herald of God's glory. In Isaiah, the meaning intensifies: the divine messenger announces God's salvation to the poor (Isaiah 61:1) and to Jerusalem (Isaiah 40:9). The word always expresses a transmission of information, but it increases in spiritual value according to the context: military news, then joy of victory, then announcement of eternal salvation.
H1319.portee: This word opens to the Christian reader what it means to be a "messenger" of the good news. Beyond mere reporting, it is about communicating a transforming joy: that of salvation in Jesus Christ. The Church receives the responsibility to "publish" or "preach" this news to all nations, not out of obligatory duty, but out of overflowing enthusiasm from one who has received grace. The word also reminds us that the announcement of the Gospel is never a secret kept: it must be shouted, shared, publicly proclaimed.

sens: The soft part of the body, covered with skin, composed of muscles and tissues
The entire body of a person or an animal
The food that consists of the meat of an animal
The ties of kinship and covenant, family
Humanity or human nature in its fragility and distance from God
All living beings, particularly animals
H1320.detail:
1. Flesh is primarily the physical substance of the body: living tissue distinct from bone and skin. When God created Eve, he made a woman "from the flesh" taken from Adam's rib (Genesis 2:21), which shows that flesh is the material of human creation.
2. It also designates the entire body, the person in their physical reality: one who "washes their body" after touching something unclean must wash completely (Leviticus 16:26).
3. Flesh becomes food when it is meat: one can "eat the flesh" of sacrifices or livestock (Jeremiah 7:21, Exodus 12:8).
4. When one says "you are my bone and my flesh," it expresses kinship and covenant (Judges 9:2): common flesh symbolizes the blood bond.
5. In the Bible, "the flesh" sometimes refers to human fragility before God: "all flesh" will perish, it is transient and sinful (Genesis 6:3, 6:12).
6. The word also applies to all animals: "all living flesh" includes beasts, birds, everything that has breath of life (Genesis 7:15).
H1320.origine: The Hebrew word בָּשָׂר comes from a root that fundamentally means what is "soft" or "fleshy," as opposed to bone. This image of living, flexible, and perishable matter is at the heart of the meaning of the word. In Aramaic, the form is identical (בְּשַׁר). The word belongs to the same family as several terms designating parts of the body, and it is often used to speak of the contrast between fragile flesh and the power or eternity of God.
H1320.emploi: The word "flesh" appears 241 times in the Hebrew text of the Bible, mostly in the Torah and historical books. It initially has a concrete anatomical sense: Moses speaks of the grain "fat with flesh" in Egypt (Genesis 41:2), or the Law details skin diseases that affect the flesh (Leviticus 13, a recurring passage). It then takes on a collective and familial sense: "bone and flesh" means "family" (Genesis 29:14). In prophetic and wisdom texts, it designates all humanity in its fragile and mortal condition: "all flesh" will see salvation or will face judgment. In sacrificial contexts, it is the matter of the meat offered or consumed according to purity rules.
H1320.portee: Understanding the word "flesh" sheds light on the biblical view of the body: it is not despised, but recognized as created, fragile, and called to obey God. The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in the New Testament takes up this distinction: flesh is humanity in itself, dependent and perishable. By reading that "all flesh" will perish or that God has compassion on those who are "flesh," the believer finds himself in a common reality: he is a created, temporal being, called not to despise his body, but to submit it to God.

sens: Physical substance of the body, muscles and living tissues
Living creature, animated being
Body of man, in its physical integrity
Humanity, the whole of mankind in their mortal condition
H1321.detail:
1. Flesh refers to the living matter that covers the bones and makes up the animal or human body. In Daniel 7:5, the bear that the king sees in vision "eats a lot of flesh": it is the very substance of the bodies that it devours.
2. The word can also refer to a living being as a whole, an animated creature. In Daniel 4:12, "every living thing" drew its food from the magnificent tree: here, "flesh" refers to any creature that lives and breathes.
3. Flesh sometimes represents the human body in its physical reality, what is visible and tangible. In Daniel 2:11, the gods do not have flesh among men: they do not inhabit the physical, visible world like humans do.
4. In a broader sense, flesh can evoke all of humanity, men in their condition of mortality and fragility, confronted with limits that only gods are unaware of.
H1321.origine: In Aramaic, בְּשַׁר (beshar) is the definite form of the word בְּשַׁר (beshar) which literally means "flesh". This word comes from the same root as the Hebrew בָּשָׂר (basar), attested many times in the Old Testament to denote animal or human flesh. The root expresses the idea of what is tender, living, flexible — the mobile and fleshy substance of the living body.
H1321.emploi: This Aramaic word appears three times in the book of Daniel, which is partly written in Aramaic (chapters 2 to 7). In Daniel 2:11, it expresses the absence of a physical body for the gods — they alone can respond to the king, as humans are limited by their condition as "fleshly" creatures. In Daniel 4:12, it designates every living being that draws its life from the nourishing tree: the word emphasizes vital dependence. In Daniel 7:5, it literally describes the substance that the animal devours — the bear eats flesh. Through these three uses, the word always expresses physical, corporeal, fleshly reality, both in humans and in beasts.
H1321.portee: This word reminds the reader that humans, unlike God and the gods of the nations, are corporeal and limited creatures. It is an invitation to recognize our mortal and fleshly condition, neither shameful nor glorious in itself, but simply the condition that God has given us. In the face of earthly kings and powers, it also reminds us that only God can truly satisfy the questions posed by the human heart.

sens: Feeling of embarrassment and dishonor caused by a shameful act or humiliating situation
State of confusion and humiliation in the face of others' judgment
Dishonor, disgrace, and loss of public reputation
Shameful or despicable thing that brings ridicule
What inspires disgust and infamy
H1322.detail:
1. Shame is primarily the personal feeling of embarrassment and dishonor: one who has acted wrongly feels embarrassed and confused about their actions. When Saul reproaches Jonathan for his friendship with David, he speaks of "shame" — it is the public affront that affects the dignity of the king and his family (1 Samuel 20:30).
2. It is also the state of humiliation one falls into when unmasked or defeated: the thief caught in the act, confused and unable to defend himself (Jeremiah 2:26), experiences this public shame.
3. The word denotes lasting disgrace, the dishonor that attaches to a person or a people: Israel will accumulate shame and ignominy if it seeks help from foreign powers (Isaiah 30:5).
4. Sometimes, shame is attributed to the object of worship itself: idols, called "shames" or "abominations", are despicable and dishonorable things to worship (Jeremiah 11:13).
5. In prophetic laments, shame becomes synonymous with the worst misfortune: it ravages life, clothes itself upon the one who suffers it, and symbolizes divine judgment (Psalms 35:26, Psalms 70:4).
H1322.origine: The Hebrew word בֹּשֶׁת (boshet) comes from the root בּוש (bush), which means "to be confused, to blush, to be afraid". This root evokes the image of a face that turns red, a visible sign of embarrassment and shame. The word appears in various forms: the verb "to blush with shame", the noun "shame" or "confusion", and the adjective "shameful, confused". In Jeremiah 11:13, "idols" also translates this word, as idols are considered shames, abominations that dishonor those who worship them.
H1322.emploi: The word shame appears about 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and the prophets. In historical accounts (1 Samuel 20:30), it denotes the personal affront suffered by a king. In the lament Psalms, it takes on the image of clothing or covering that envelops the one who suffers (Psalms 35:26, Psalms 69:20, Psalms 109:29). In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel), shame becomes collective and future: it is the punishment promised to Israel or to rebellious peoples. In Jeremiah 11:13 and Hosea 9:10, it qualifies the idols themselves, highlighting divine disgust at false worship. The personal feeling of private shame gradually expands to public shame and divine judgment on the nations.
H1322.portee: Biblical shame is not just a fleeting emotion: it symbolizes the distance from God and the consequence of sin. Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible views judgment — not as an abstraction, but as a public humiliation before all, a loss of prestige and dignity. Conversely, Jesus Christ removes the shame from those who follow him (Isaiah 54:4): he restores lost honor. That is why so many Psalms pray for shame to fall upon God's enemies — not out of personal vengeance, but because shame is the sign of just judgment.

sens: Female child, born of a father and a mother
Woman, especially a young woman or woman from a specific region
Descendant, granddaughter, or woman of a later generation
Term of affection or respect towards a woman
Villages or dependencies of a main city
Personification of a city or community
H1323G.detail:
1. The primary meaning is female child: God created men and women, and from the earliest generations "he fathered sons and daughters" (Genesis 5:4). This is the direct parental relationship from the father or mother to the daughter.
2. The word expands to encompass any woman, especially a young one, without obligatory kinship: a "daughter" can refer to a woman from a given city or people, as when Solomon takes "many foreign women" from the Moabites and Sidonians (1 Kings 11:1).
3. It can also express distant descent: a "daughter" is then the daughter of an ancestor, a granddaughter, or a descendant of the people.
4. In affectionate or solemn language, a woman whom one wishes to honor or encourage is called "daughter": the psalmist says "Listen, my daughter" to address the queen tenderly (Psalms 45:11).
5. In geography, the "daughters" of a city are the villages and small settlements that depend on it.
6. Finally, the Bible personifies cities or peoples as women: the "daughters" of Moab refers to the entire Moabite people and their women taken into captivity (Jeremiah 48:46).
H1323G.origine: The Hebrew word בַּת (bat) comes from a very ancient root meaning "to give birth" or "to bear children." It is related to other words in the Semitic family. In Aramaic, a similar word with the same meaning is found. The parallel with the Greek θυγάτηρ (thugátèr) shows that this notion of female child was universal in antiquity. This term has gained nuances over time: from the strict meaning of biological daughter to the broader sense of woman, and even to the poetic notion of personification of a city or collective entity.
H1323G.emploi: The word appears 474 times in the Old Testament, demonstrating its importance. It is prominent from Genesis, where it describes the children of the first humans (Genesis 5), and then it enriches various contexts: marital unions (Genesis 24:23, where one asks "who are you?"), family relationships and genealogies, legal situations concerning virginity (Deuteronomy 22:17). In the Psalms and the Prophets, the word takes on broader dimensions, encompassing the women of a community or serving to personify entire cities. For example, "the daughters of Moab" (Jeremiah 48:46) does not only refer to children but to all the women of the kingdom, expressed as a feminine collective. Secondary translations (ostrich, branch) likely reflect homophones or rare metaphorical uses.
H1323G.portee: This simple and fundamental word reminds us that God creates men and women in His image, and that no distinction of value exists between them: daughters inherit, are loved, and receive prophetic words just like sons. Understanding that the Bible affectionately calls a woman "daughter" (as in "Listen, my daughter") shows how God addresses us all as His beloved children, with tenderness and benevolent authority.

sens: Village or small town dependent on a larger city
Satellite settlement of a mother city
H1323H.detail:
1. In the Old Testament, the word refers to small localities that revolve around a large fortified city. These daughter cities are administratively and militarily subordinate to it. For example, Ekron and its daughter cities (Joshua 15:45) formed a group where the main city was the dominant center. Similarly, Beth-Shean and the cities of its jurisdiction (1 Chronicles 7:29) illustrate this urban hierarchy: the main city controlled the surrounding towns.
2. The term also applies to settlements grouped around a metropolis: Heshbon and all the cities of its jurisdiction (Numbers 21:25) or Megiddo and the cities of its jurisdiction (1 Chronicles 7:29). These dependent villages ensured the supply and defense of the territory under the jurisdiction of the mother city.
H1323H.origine: The Hebrew word bat literally means "daughter" and comes from a root expressing the idea of offspring or dependence. Its use to designate satellite cities is based on an image: just as a daughter belongs to her natal home and depends on her father, a small city belongs to its mother city and depends on it. This familial metaphor reflects the political and administrative structure of the ancient Near East. The same word bat is used to refer to women, but here it applies to the hierarchical relationship between settlements.
H1323H.emploi: This term appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Joshua, Judges, and 1 Chronicles, during descriptions of conquests and land distributions in the Promised Land. It is also found in Nehemiah during the return from exile. The expression "the cities of its jurisdiction" is formulaic and recurrent: it systematically appears in territorial lists to indicate that a city does not exist in isolation but commands dependent villages. This structure reflects the administrative organization of Canaanite and Israelite society: each fortified city governed the towns and hamlets of its territory.
H1323H.portee: This word reminds us that in the Old Testament, power and administration are organized according to a natural hierarchy of centers and peripheries. It also shows how Scripture concretely describes the political and territorial life of the chosen people: not as an abstract system, but as a collection of living cities with their dependencies. For the Christian reader, this is a detail that anchors the story of salvation in measurable historical and geographical reality.

sens: Canaanite woman, wife of Judah and mother of his first three sons Er, Onan, and Shelah
H1323I.detail: 1. Bat-Shua (the name means "daughter of Shua") is a Canaanite woman who married Judah, the son of Jacob. She bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er, her firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord and was struck dead (1 Chronicles 2:3).
H1323I.origine: The name "Bat-Shua" comes from the Hebrew "bat" meaning "daughter" and "Shua," which was the name of her father. In Genesis, this character is identified as the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, highlighting Judah's marriage to a foreigner from his family.
H1323I.emploi: Bat-Shua appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:3, where she is presented as Judah's wife and the mother of Judah's first three sons mentioned in the genealogy. This brief mention places her story within the lineage of Judah, which will later be that of King David and the Messiah.
H1323I.portee: The story of Bat-Shua reminds us that the ancestors of God's people married women from other nations and that God worked through imperfect human families. Her sons, particularly her descendants, are part of the genealogical chain leading to Jesus.

sens: Unit of measurement for liquid capacity
Quantity of wine, oil, or water measured in baths
Approximately 40 liters or 9 imperial gallons
H1324.detail:
1. The bath is a Hebrew unit of measurement intended for measuring liquids such as water, wine, or oil. It is the liquid equivalent of the ephah, which measures solids. In 1 Kings 7:38, each bronze basin of the Temple contained forty baths, indicating that the bath was used to quantify large volumes.

2. The bath is concretely used to assess deliveries and harvests. In 2 Chronicles 2:10, King Solomon receives twenty thousand baths of wine and twenty thousand baths of oil as tribute for the construction of the Temple, illustrating its administrative and commercial use.

3. The bath corresponds to approximately 40 liters (or 9 imperial gallons according to ancient sources). This capacity makes it comparable to our modern buckets or barrels, large enough for the storage and provisions of households or sanctuaries.
H1324.origine: The Hebrew word bat comes from a root expressing the idea of filling or containing. It exists in Aramaic in the same form. The bath and the ephah are the two basic units of the biblical metric system: the ephah for grains and solids, the bath for liquids. This symmetry shows the importance of a coherent measurement system in Israelite life.
H1324.emploi: The word bath appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in texts describing Solomon's Temple and its utensils (1 Kings 7), the tributes to the king (2 Chronicles 2), and the measurement laws prescribed by the prophet Ezekiel for the ideal temple (Ezekiel 45). In Isaiah 5:10, Isaiah uses the bath to illustrate the meager harvests promised in judgment: an entire vineyard will produce only one bath of wine. Ezekiel 45:10-11 emphasizes the need for a just bath, reflecting biblical concerns for commercial fairness and cultic integrity.
H1324.portee: The bath reminds us that God cares about the material details of everyday life: He ordains justice in measurements and penalizes fraud. For the Christian, this underscores that integrity in small things (honesty in trade, adherence to standards) reflects faithfulness to God. The bath also illustrates how the ancient realities of Israelite worship (its utensils, its measurements) foreshadowed the precision and order that Jesus would bring.

sens: Hebrew unit of measurement for liquids
Approximately 40 liters of capacity
Measure corresponding to the ephah for dry materials
H1325.detail:
1. The bath is a unit of measurement used in the Old Testament to quantify liquids, particularly wine and oil. The text of Ezra 7:22 clearly shows this: the king of Persia authorizes the bringing to Jerusalem of "one hundred baths of wine" and "one hundred baths of oil," indicating that these are large quantities of valuable products.

2. One bath represents approximately 40 liters, making it a significant volume for trade and religious offerings. It is a substantial quantity, not just a handful or a small pot.

3. The bath corresponds in the Hebrew metric system to the ephah for dry measurements (such as wheat). The two units are equivalent in volume, demonstrating consistency in the measurement system used in Israel.
H1325.origine: The Hebrew word bat (בַּת) is also used in the sense of "daughter" in biblical Hebrew, from which its root derives. Here, in the context of measurement, bat specifically denotes a unit of measurement for liquids. This term was common in the ancient Near East for assessing supplies of oil and wine, essential commodities for daily life and temple services.
H1325.emploi: The bath appears infrequently in the Old Testament. Its primary usage is found in Ezra 7:22, where King Artaxerxes, authorizing the funding of the temple in Jerusalem, specifies the quantities of oil and wine to be provided, measured in baths. This technical term belongs to the administrative and commercial vocabulary of the times of exile and restoration. It shows how, even after the exile, the Israelites maintained standardized measurements for temple provisions.
H1325.portee: This word reminds us of the practical importance of temple life: God cares that His sanctuary is adequately supplied with oil and wine for worship. The exact quantities mentioned (one hundred baths) demonstrate the order and precision that God desires in religious service, and how even a foreign power recognizes the importance of providing for the needs of the Jerusalem temple.

sens: State of land left abandoned, becoming desolate and barren
Destruction, annihilation of a work or prosperity
H1326.detail:
1. The word describes a field or vineyard that falls into decay: the walls collapse, the crops disappear, only thorns and brambles remain. It is the image of total abandonment. In Isaiah 5:6, God threatens to reduce His vineyard "to ruin," ceasing to care for it and ordering that no rain fall upon it — the contrast is striking with the care He had taken at the beginning of the passage.
2. More broadly, the word expresses the destruction of what was built, prosperous, and alive. It is the annihilation of a blessing, the return to chaos and barrenness.
H1326.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking collapse and devastation. It belongs to a family of terms that describe the state of what has collapsed or disappeared — a ruined field is one where order and life have given way to disorder and death.
H1326.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 5:6, in a famous prophetic parable. There, God explains how He will abandon His beloved vineyard — a symbol of the people of Israel — to destruction. The context is that of divine judgment: ruin is not the result of chance or wear, but of God's deliberate action in withdrawing His protection and care.
H1326.portee: This word reminds the reader that the absence of divine care, the abandonment of the relationship with God, leads to ruin. But it is also a warning: the image of the destroyed vineyard calls for vigilance and faithfulness. It also shows that God does not destroy out of malice, but because the people have ceased to produce the fruit He expected.

sens: Steep and rugged rock face
Desolate and wild place with steep slopes
H1327.detail: 1. The word designates a sheer rock face, a very steep cliff that is not easily climbed. In Isaiah 7:19, the wasps will come to settle "in the clefts of the rocks" — these clefts that carve the steep walls — and in the desolate valleys: the image is one of rocky, rugged terrain formed of steep and inhospitable slopes. 2. By extension, the word evokes a barren and abandoned place, far from civilization, where desolation and silence reign: it is the haunt of wild beasts and insects, not of men.
H1327.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of rupture and tearing: a wall that rises abruptly, cut off sharply. The word is related to terms meaning "separation" or "destruction." It paints the image of a fractured terrain, where the rock stands as impassable walls.
H1327.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 7:19. It describes the desert landscape where the Lord will send the wasps as punishment: the creatures that will ravage the land will gather in the most arid and rocky places, the precipices and inaccessible valleys. This choice underscores the extent of the judgment — even the most remote spaces will not be spared.
H1327.portee: This word reminds us that God controls all of creation, even the smallest and most remote creatures, and that He can use them to accomplish His purposes. The precipice, a place of desolation, becomes an instrument of divine judgment.

sens: Man of Abraham's family, living in the time of the Patriarchs
Father of Rebecca and Laban
Son of Nahor and Milcah
H1328A.detail: Bethuel is a man who lived during the time of the Patriarchs, belonging to Abraham's close family. He is the son of Nahor (Abraham's brother) and Milcah, making him Abraham's nephew. In the story of Rebecca, he plays an important role: he is the one who gives his daughter Rebecca in marriage to Isaac, Abraham's son. Although few words are attributed to him in the Bible, Bethuel is a key figure in the account of Genesis 24, where Abraham's servant comes to find a wife for Isaac. When the servant presents his plan, Bethuel and his son Laban recognize that "the matter comes from the Lord" (Genesis 24:50), thus accepting the marriage according to God's will.
H1328A.origine: The name Bethuel means "God destroys" or "man of God" or "dwells in God." It is composed of two elements that refer to divinity and divine action. Bethuel belongs to the genealogy of Nahor, Abraham's brother, placing him in the branch of the family that remained in Mesopotamia, far from the land of Canaan that God had promised to Abraham.
H1328A.emploi: Bethuel appears 9 times in the Bible, all in Genesis. He is first mentioned in the genealogy of Nahor (Genesis 22:22-23), where he is presented as the father of Rebecca. His main role is played in the account of Rebecca's marriage to Isaac (Genesis 24), where Abraham's servant meets him and discusses with him and Laban to obtain Rebecca in marriage. Bethuel is also mentioned when Rebecca leaves her family to join Isaac. He is a figure of transition: he remains in Mesopotamia, far from the people of the Covenant, but he recognizes the action of the Lord when it manifests and he agrees to release his daughter so that she may be part of God's plan.
H1328A.portee: Bethuel embodies divine providence that acts beyond the borders of the chosen people. Although he lives far from Canaan and does not follow God's call as Abraham did, he remains sensitive to divine will and willing to submit to it. His story reminds us that God directs history and gathers His people according to His purposes, even using men who are not at the heart of the Covenant. For the Christian, Bethuel illustrates how God can use ordinary people, far from His central revelation, to fulfill His promises.

sens: City in the territory of Simeon in southern Israel
H1328B.detail: Bethuel is a fortified locality that belongs to the tribe of Simeon, in the southern region of the territory of Israel. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in a list of cities of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:30), alongside Hormah and Ziklag, two other cities in the Negev.
H1328B.origine: The Hebrew name Bethuel literally means "house of God" or "God destroys" according to ancient etymological interpretations. It is composed of two elements: the root "beth" which means "house" or "place," and a derivative of the divine name "El" (God), or from a verb expressing destruction. This type of geographical name composed with "beth" and a divine name was common in Hebrew onomastics.
H1328B.emploi: Bethuel appears only once in the provided biblical usages: in 1 Chronicles 4:30, where it is listed among the fortified cities attributed to the tribe of Simeon. This list is part of the tribal and geographical census of the territory of Israel after the settlement in Canaan. Its presence alongside other cities of the Negev indicates its importance as an established locality in the southern part of the country.

sens: City of the tribe of Simeon in Palestine
H1329.detail: Bethul is a small city in southern Palestine assigned to the tribe of Simeon during the division of the territory after the conquest. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, listed among the cities that Simeon received as an inheritance (Joshua 19:4), between Eltolad and Hormah.
H1329.origine: The Hebrew name בְּתוּל (betul) likely means "dwells in God" or "God destroys," composed of roots evoking either a house or a place of habitation, or divine action. It is a theophoric name — a name containing a reference to God — which was common in ancient Israel for cities and people.
H1329.emploi: Bethul appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:4, in the list of fortified cities of the tribe of Simeon. This list enumerates the territories that God assigned to Simeon after its initial domain was reduced — other tribes received larger portions, and Simeon received its inheritance enclosed within the southern territory of Judah.

sens: young girl who has never had sexual relations
young girl, young woman in general
woman or city personified as fiancée or wife
innocence and fragility in the face of danger
H1330.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a young girl who has not known a man in the biblical sense. Genesis 24:16 states of Rebecca: "She was very beautiful to behold; she was a virgin, and no man had known her." It is the absence of sexual relations that defines this status.
2. By natural extension, the word applies to any young girl or young woman, whether or not her virginity is emphasized. In Deuteronomy 32:25, it simply describes young women facing misfortune, without intending to highlight their sexual status, just as in Isaiah 23:4, where Sidon speaks of the young girls she has raised.
3. Metaphorically, virgins and cities are treated as fragile brides: Jeremiah 31:4 calls Israel "Virgin of Israel," referring to her as the beloved wife of the Lord. Lamentations speaks of the "virgins of Jerusalem" in mourning, likening the city to a broken young woman.
4. The word also evokes vulnerability: virgins are particularly exposed to violence (Lamentations 2:10, 5:11), reinforcing the image of weakness and innocence that requires protection.
H1330.origine: The Hebrew word בְּתוּלָה (betulah) comes from a root meaning separation or distinction — the idea of a young girl set apart, reserved. It originally describes the state of an unmarried and sexually intact woman. The word belongs to a family that expresses youth and separation from the group of older women. It was commonly used in the ancient East to denote a specific social and familial status.
H1330.emploi: The word appears fifty times in the Old Testament, especially in the texts of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy), where it defines rights and duties (Exodus 22:16-17 addresses the case of a seduced virgin). The prophets often use it figuratively: Israel is called "Virgin of Israel" (Jeremiah 31:4) or Jerusalem "virgin of Jerusalem" (Lamentations 2:10), thus designating the beloved of the Lord or the devastated city. In the psalms and narratives (Esther, Samuel), it simply describes young women in their youth and fragility. The word thus shifts from the strict sense (sexual integrity) to the broader sense (youth, innocence, vulnerability).
H1330.portee: This word reminds us that virginity in the Old Testament is not an abstract morality, but a concrete reality linked to family honor and the order of marriage. For the Christian reader, the use of the word to designate Israel or Jerusalem invites reflection on the relationship God desires with His people: a faithful and exclusive intimacy, tinged with tenderness toward the one who is trusting and fragile. The term also reassures that throughout the Bible, God protects and restores vulnerable young women.

sens: State of one who has never had sexual relations
Total absence of sexual experience before marriage
Moral purity and marital integrity
Mark of honor and social respect for a young woman
H1331.detail:
1. Virginity primarily refers to the physical and moral state of someone who has never had sexual intercourse. It is the integrity of the body before marriage. In Deuteronomy 22:14, a man accuses his new wife of not being "a virgin," a serious accusation concerning her initial status.

2. Closely related to the above, the word evokes the carnal innocence that precedes marriage. When the daughter of the leader Jephthah goes to weep for "her virginity" in the mountains (Judges 11:37), she mourns the loss of what would have marked her nuptial honor.

3. Virginity also has a moral and spiritual dimension: it is the absence of defilement and guilt. The "signs of virginity" that parents present before the elders (Deuteronomy 22:15, 22:17) are tangible proof of this intact honor.

4. Socially and legally, it is a marital asset and a marker of respectability. In the laws of Deuteronomy 22, it conditions rights and honor: a husband cannot divorce a legally married virgin, and falsely accusing a woman of not being a virgin is punishable.
H1331.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that evokes youth and puberty. It properly designates the state of one who enters adulthood without having known marriage. The precise form of the word suggests a lasting state or condition — that of an unmarried and sexually intact young person. It is a concrete word, rooted in bodily and social reality.
H1331.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Law (Deuteronomy, Leviticus) and in historical narratives. In Leviticus 21:13, it simply refers to the condition a priest must seek in his wife. But Deuteronomy 22:14-20 makes it a heavy legal subject: a husband who falsely accuses his wife of not being a virgin incurs penalties (fines, prohibition of divorce); it is a matter of family honor and rights. In Judges 11:37, Jephthah's daughter uses the word to express her personal mourning — she will never marry and thus lose this status. Ezekiel 23:3 and 23:8 apply the image to Israel and Judah, their respective virginities and their spiritual adultery against God.
H1331.portee: This word shows us how seriously Scripture takes the integrity of the body and purity before marriage. It is not just a social taboo: it is a reality protected by the Law. For Christians, Paul's passage in 1 Corinthians 7 values chastity before marriage. This word reminds us that God honors those who keep their bodies pure, not out of legalism, but out of self-respect and respect for the one they will love.

sens: Daughter of a Pharaoh of Egypt
Wife of the Jew Mered
Mother of three sons: Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah
H1332.detail:
1. Bithiah is an Egyptian woman, daughter of Pharaoh, living during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. She appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:18, where she is explicitly referred to as "daughter of Pharaoh."

2. She marries Mered, a man from the tribe of Judah. This marriage between an Egyptian princess and a Jew is remarkable and shows the familial ties that could exist between Egypt and the kingdom of Judah at that time.

3. She is the mother of three children: Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah. These Hebrew names indicate that her sons were fully integrated into the genealogy of Israel.
H1332.origine: The name Bithiah means "daughter of Jehovah" (or "daughter of the Lord"), composed of "bat" (daughter) and the divine name. It is a name that contrasts remarkably with her status as daughter of Pharaoh: it perhaps suggests an adherence to the faith of Israel, or at least a particular divine blessing for this Egyptian woman integrated into the people of God. The fact that she is given this theophoric name underscores the importance of her role in the genealogy of Judah.
H1332.emploi: Bithiah appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:18. She is mentioned in the genealogies of the clan of Judah, among the descendants of Caleb. Her inclusion in this genealogy shows that she is regarded as a mother of the house of Judah, despite her Egyptian origin. The Bible explicitly designates her as "daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took as wife," which situates her historically and socially and illustrates the marital alliances between the ancient kingdoms of the Near East.
H1332.portee: The mention of Bithiah reminds us that God incorporates into His people foreigners who embrace His faith and lineage. Although she is the daughter of Pharaoh, she becomes a mother in Israel, and her descendants are integrated into the genealogy of Judah. Her story invites the reader to see that faith and covenant with the Lord transcend national boundaries and royal statuses.

sens: To stab repeatedly
To perforate, to go through from one side to the other
H1333.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of stabbing someone with repeated blows, especially with a sharp weapon — to pierce, to stab multiple times. In Ezekiel 16:40, the unfaithful city of Jerusalem is threatened with being "pierced with the sword": the image is that of a multitude of wounds inflicted successively.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of going through something from one side to the other, of perforating or cutting into pieces. It is a violent and repeated act that progressively destroys.
H1333.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּתַק (bataq) comes from a root that literally means "to cut, to slice." The Piel (intensive form used here) emphasizes the idea of repetition or multiplicity: not just a single cut, but several blows delivered together. The word conveys the image of a brutal attack with sharp weapons, blows that perforate.
H1333.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 16:40. It is found in a context of divine punishment: God announces to Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful woman, that she will be attacked by a crowd that would stone her and pierce her with the sword. This dramatic passage underscores the violence of the judgment incurred for unfaithfulness.
