H1333.portee: This word reminds us of the seriousness of divine judgment on sin and unfaithfulness to the covenant. It invites the reader not to take lightly the rupture with God: the consequences are terrible. At the same time, the prophetic context also invites repentance, the only way to avoid such punishment.

sens: to divide into two parts with a sharp blow
to separate the pieces of a slaughtered animal
H1334.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of cutting something in one blow to divide it into two parts. It is a clean and decisive gesture, as one would cut a branch or a trunk. In Genesis 15:10, Abram "cuts" the sacrificial animals in half, creating two distinct halves.
2. More concretely, it involves dividing an animal into distinct pieces: separating the body parts of a slaughtered animal to make portions. The sacrificial context of Genesis 15 clearly shows this separation of the animals in two, each piece placed facing the other, which was a common practice in the covenant rituals of the time.
H1334.origine: The Hebrew verb bâtar comes from a root that expresses the idea of division and clear separation. The basic image is that of a cut that slices, definitively separating two parts. This word belongs to the vocabulary of ritual and domestic gestures: to slaughter, to cut, to share.
H1334.emploi: The verb appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. Its only use in Genesis 15:10 occurs at the heart of the narrative where God establishes a covenant with Abram. This passage describes the preparation of the sacrificial animal according to the customs of the time: the animal is slaughtered, cut in two so that the parts remain facing each other. It is in this space between the two halves that Abram will see the divine presence, sealing the covenant. The act of cutting thus carries a profound symbolic and religious value.
H1334.portee: This gesture of dividing the animals reminds the reader that the covenant with God is not a mere agreement: it is a solid commitment, marked by an impressive and memorable rite. The cutting of the animal signifies that what is separated cannot be recomposed — the covenant is definitive. For the Christian, this moment foreshadows the ultimate sacrifice of Christ, who establishes the new covenant through the shedding of His blood.

sens: Part of an animal cut in two for a sacrifice or rite
Each of the halves of an animal separated by a cut in the middle
Piece resulting from the division of a victim
H1335.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a part of an animal that has been cut in two. In Genesis 15:10, Abram "cut in the middle" the sacrificial animals and "set each piece opposite the other": these are the two halves of the same beast, divided horizontally. It is a very concrete act, visible to the eyes.
2. This piece has a primarily ritual function: it is an act of covenant. In Jeremiah 34:18-19, passing between the pieces of a calf cut in two is a rite of solemn commitment. Those who "pass between the pieces" accept the conditions of the covenant; anyone who violates them incurs a punishment similar to that of the calf.
3. The word thus takes on a figurative meaning: the piece becomes the visible sign of a binding promise, and even the putting one's own life at stake. Violating the covenant means deserving the fate of the calf.
H1335.origine: The Hebrew word בֶּתֶר (bèter) likely comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to separate." It first describes the physical action of dividing, then the piece that results from it. In the Greek Old Testament, it is often translated by a word meaning "part" or "piece." This notion of division and separation is at the heart of the covenant rite: cutting the animal in two symbolizes the commitment of the one who passes between its halves.
H1335.emploi: The word appears only three times, all in the context of the covenant. In Genesis 15:10, it is the concrete rite of Abram before God, who is about to seal a covenant with him. In Jeremiah 34:18-19, the same rite returns, but this time to denounce those who have violated the covenant: they passed between the pieces without honoring their commitment. The word remains closely linked to this solemn gesture and its consequences. It is a technical term in the vocabulary of the ancient covenant.
H1335.portee: This word helps us understand how our ancestors in faith took their commitments seriously. Passing between the pieces of a cut beast was to say: "May I be like this calf if I betray my word." The piece was thus a pledge of life or death. This shows how serious and foundational faithfulness to the covenant was. For the Christian, this enriches the understanding of the new covenant in Christ: God's covenants have always cost something.

sens: mountainous region of Palestine, characterized by its peaks and steep valleys
H1336.detail: Béter designates a mountainous region of Palestine, probably located east of Jerusalem. The name itself evokes rocky peaks, ridges, and crevices that fragment the terrain. In Song of Solomon 2:17, the beloved husband flees "on the mountains of Béter" like a bounding gazelle, a poetic image where this mountainous and steep landscape highlights the wild beauty and lightness of movement.
H1336.origine: The Hebrew word Béter (בֶּתֶר) derives from a root meaning "to split" or "to tear." It thus evokes fissured mountains, cut by ravines and gorges — a land fragmented by geography. This descriptive name reflects the rugged character of the Palestinian terrain.
H1336.emploi: Béter appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:17. In this poetic and romantic context, the mountainous region of Béter symbolizes a remote, wild, and difficult-to-access place — exactly the setting where the young girl imagines her beloved fleeing lightly, like a gazelle on the ridges. The proper name evokes both remoteness and grandeur.
H1336.portee: This passage from the Song invites contemplation of the beauty of created nature — the steep mountains of Béter — as a reflection of love and grace. It is a call to recognize the Creator in the splendor of His work.

sens: Gate of the city of Heshbon
H1337.detail: 1. Bath-Rabbim is a gate of the city of Heshbon, in the Promised Land. Its name literally means "daughter of the multitudes" — a poetic expression that likely evokes the bustle and flow of people passing through this gate. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:5, where the lovesick poet compares the eyes of his beloved to the "pools of Heshbon, near the gate of Bath-Rabbim."
H1337.origine: The name Bath-Rabbim is composed of two Hebrew words: *bat* ("daughter") and *rabbim* ("multitudes" or "many"). It is a typical poetic appellation in Hebrew, personifying places by calling them "daughters" — just as "daughter of Zion" refers to Jerusalem. The name suggests a gate famous for the crowd that circulated there.
H1337.emploi: Bath-Rabbim appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 7:5. This context is purely poetic and lyrical: the beloved praises the beauty of his companion by comparing her eyes to the pools that extend near this gate of Heshbon. The choice of this particular gate reveals the poet's knowledge of the real and prestigious places of Canaan, but the intention is entirely aesthetic and romantic, not historical or geographical.

sens: region of the Jordan Valley, east of the river
H1338.detail: Bithron is a region or district located in the Jordan Valley, on the eastern bank of the river. Its name suggests a notion of division or fracture of the terrain, perhaps evoking gorges or ravines characteristic of this area. It is through this region that Abner and his troops pass during their nighttime retreat (2 Samuel 2:29), indicating that it is a traversable but likely rugged territory.
H1338.origine: The name Bithron derives from a Hebrew root meaning "to divide" or "to split." It evokes the geographical aspect of the region: a terrain cut by ravines or faults, characteristic of certain valleys of the Jordan. This name thus describes less a city than a territory defined by its particular topography.
H1338.emploi: Bithron appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 2:29. It serves as a geographical landmark during the military movements following Saul's death. Abner crosses this region with his men to go to Mahanaim, indicating that Bithron was a known and frequented passage. Its location in the Jordan Valley, east of the river, places it in Israelite territory after the conquest.

sens: woman of Israel during the time of the united monarchy, wife of King David
mother of King Solomon
H1339.detail: Bathsheba is a woman living in the time of King David. She is first mentioned as the wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 11:3), then she becomes the wife of King David after he seduces her and has Uriah killed in battle. She gives birth to Solomon, who becomes king and is loved by the Lord (2 Samuel 12:24). Later, she intervenes with the aging King David to ensure that Solomon is recognized as his successor, thus demonstrating her political influence and role in the royal succession (1 Kings 1:11-31).
H1339.origine: The name means "daughter of an oath" in Hebrew (bath = daughter, sheba = oath). Bathsheba is also referred to as Bath-shua in some passages (1 Chronicles 3:5), a variant of the same name.
H1339.emploi: Bathsheba appears 11 times in the Old Testament, primarily in 2 Samuel 11-12 and 1 Kings 1-2. She is first presented as the wife of Uriah, an officer of David, before becoming the king's wife. Her story illustrates both King David's sin and divine mercy: although conceived in sin, her son Solomon becomes a great king. Bathsheba plays a key role in the kingdom's politics by supporting Solomon's succession against his older brother Adonijah, making her a figure of wisdom and influence in the royal court.
H1339.portee: The story of Bathsheba reveals that even in the midst of a moral tragedy—the sin of adultery and murder—God's grace remains active. It also shows the dignity and intelligence of a woman capable of influencing the events of the kingdom to fulfill God's plan, reminding the reader that God works through people, even in the most complicated circumstances.

sens: Woman married successively to Uriah and to David
Mother of Solomon and other sons of David
Daughter of Ammiel
Wife of the king of Judah (alternative spelling of Bathsheba)
H1340.detail:
1. Bath-Sheba is the wife of Uriah, an officer of David. After Uriah's death, she becomes David's wife and the mother of several royal children. The account in 2 Samuel 11 narrates the events that lead to her marriage to the king.

2. She is the mother of Solomon, who will become king after David, as well as three other sons: Shimea, Shobab, and Nathan. She is one of the most important women in the royal lineage of Israel, as she is the mother of the greatest king of the united kingdom.

3. She is the daughter of Ammiel, a man from Jerusalem mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:5. This genealogical detail anchors her in the elite of the royal capital.

4. Bath-Sheba is the alternative spelling of the name Bathsheba (which means "daughter of oaths"). Both forms of the name refer to the same woman, and she is written this way in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3:5.
H1340.origine: The name Bath-Sheba means in Hebrew "daughter of wealth" or "daughter of opulence." Bath always means "daughter" in Hebrew; Sheba refers to wealth and prosperity. This woman bears a name that evokes richness, and she is indeed linked to the royal court and the lineage of Solomon. The name is a variant spelling of Bathsheba, where Sheba means "oath." Both forms coexist in ancient Hebrew texts.
H1340.emploi: Bath-Sheba appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:5, in a genealogical list of David's children born in Jerusalem. The Chronicler lists the four sons she bore to the king: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Although this name appears only once explicitly, the woman herself is much better known as Bathsheba (H1339), which frequently appears in 2 Samuel 11-12 and 1 Kings 1-2. This woman plays a central role in the story of David's sin and in the royal succession, as she is the mother of Solomon. The genealogical passage in 1 Chronicles 3:5 acknowledges her importance by naming her among the royal wives.
H1340.portee: The account of Bath-Sheba teaches how God forgives serious sin and continues to fulfill His promises. Although David committed adultery and murder to have her, God sanctified their union by giving Solomon, the child of this relationship, the throne of Israel. This story reveals divine grace: God does not withhold His blessing because of the weaknesses of His servants, but He disciplines and restores. For the Christian, it shows that God can turn evil into good and that sincere repentance opens the door to reconciliation and the fulfillment of His plans.

sens: One who is filled with excessive pride and arrogance
Who displays their importance and despises others
Who believes themselves superior and would refuse to lower themselves
H1341.detail:
1. The word designates a person puffed up with pride, who feels great and important because of what they possess or what they believe themselves to be. In Isaiah 16:6, Moab is described as "proud": it speaks of "the pride of the proud Moab, his arrogance and his haughtiness." This is an ostentatious, displayed pride.
2. This pride is accompanied by contempt for others: the proud person believes themselves better, refuses to lower themselves, and speaks with arrogance. Moab is presented as speaking "in vain words," meaning empty words that inflate his importance.
3. It is a brazen pride that provokes the anger of God: in the same verse, this pride of Moab stands in opposition to the humility that God requires. Pride is the opposite attitude of what a believer should have before God.
H1341.origine: The Hebrew word גֵּא (ge) literally means "exalted" or "that stands up." It evokes the image of something that rises, that swells. This root is connected to the idea of physical height, and it has taken on the meaning of excessive moral height: pride. In Hebrew, this word belongs to the family of those that describe pride and arrogance.
H1341.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 16:6. It describes the pride of the kingdom of Moab at the time of Isaiah. This pride is presented as reprehensible: it is linked to the arrogance and haughtiness that characterize a people rebellious to God. The context shows that this pride heralds a fall, as God humbles the proud.
H1341.portee: This word reminds the reader that pride and arrogance are contrary to the spirit that God requires. For a believer, "pride" is an attitude to flee from: it distances one from God and provokes His judgment. Isaiah denounces the pride of Moab to show that all excessive pride without humility before God is destined for collapse.

sens: To rise, to stand up high
To grow, to increase, to augment in strength or volume
To manifest with brilliance, to shine with glory or power
To exceed a limit, to become too great or too deep
H1342.detail:
1. To rise, to stand up high: the word primarily designates the physical movement of something that goes up or stands upright. It is the concrete image: an object or a person that rises from the ground or stands up.
2. To grow, to increase, to augment in strength or volume: the word also describes natural growth, progressive expansion. Job 8:11 uses it for the rush that grows in the marsh: a plant that rises and spreads.
3. To manifest with brilliance, to shine with glory or power: when it concerns God or His action, "to rise" takes on a triumphant and glorious hue. Exodus 15:1 sings of the glory of the Lord that "breaks forth" above His enemies: it is His victory that shines.
4. To exceed a limit, to become too great or too deep: the word can qualify what exceeds human measure or capacity. Ezekiel 47:5 describes water that is "so" deep that it cannot be crossed on foot: it has risen beyond the possible.
H1342.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּאָה (gaah) has at its root the idea of "to rise" and "to be proud." It belongs to a family of words related to height, glory, and sometimes pride (גָּאוֹן, gaon, majesty or pride). The basic image is that of movement upwards, of a visible and impressive emergence.
H1342.emploi: This verb appears five times in the provided Old Testament, with nuances depending on the context. In Exodus 15:1 and 15:21, at the heart of the victory song after the crossing of the Red Sea, it expresses how the glory (or power) of the Lord "breaks forth" — it manifests itself in a brilliant and triumphant way against His enemies. In Job 8:11, it simply describes the growth of the rush in its natural environment: a neutral image of growth. In Job 10:16 and Ezekiel 47:5, the context is one of a limit exceeded or an impressive depth: the water rises "so" high that it becomes unpassable. The verb thus takes on a heroic color when it concerns God, neutral when it concerns nature, and alarming when it exceeds what can be mastered.
H1342.portee: This word teaches us that the glory of God is not hidden or murmured: it "breaks forth," it visibly manifests, it rises with power. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize the moments when God reveals Himself in history and in life. It is also a reminder that certain divine realities surpass us: they are too high, too deep to be grasped without humility.

sens: One who shows pride, who believes themselves superior to others
One who has a haughty attitude, who looks down on others
One who stands tall with pride, who lifts their head with arrogance
Rebellious towards God, who refuses to submit to His authority
H1343.detail:
1. It is the person who thinks they are worth more than others and shows it through their behavior and words. The proud person boasts, despises others, and believes they are better. In Psalms 123:4, the psalmist complains of being mocked "by the scorn of the proud": these people look down on him because they believe themselves superior.
2. It is also the attitude of one who lifts their head, who stands proudly, with arrogance. The image is that of a lofty bearing, of a judging gaze from above. In Psalms 140:6, the proud one "sets a trap": their haughty attitude is accompanied by malice towards those they despise.
3. The proud are often presented as a threat, a danger to the weak. In Proverbs 15:25, the Lord "overthrows the house of the proud" while He "establishes the boundaries of the widow": pride oppresses the small, and God opposes those who believe themselves all-powerful.
4. It is also rebellion against God: refusing to recognize His authority, placing oneself above divine law. In Job 40:6-7, God commands to "humble the proud" with "a glance", showing that pride is ultimately a crime against God, who alone is great.
H1343.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to rise" or "to stand up": it is the image of one who lifts their head, who elevates themselves. The root first expresses physical movement (the head rising, the body standing), then the accompanying moral and spiritual behavior. In the Bible, this word designates one who voluntarily places themselves above others and ultimately above God.
H1343.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah). Most uses depict the proud as a threatening figure that God combats. In the Psalms, the proud oppress and mock the righteous (Psalms 123:4, 140:6). In Proverbs and among the prophets, they are rebels whom God brings down (Proverbs 15:25, Isaiah 2:12). The word has only a negative connotation: it is always a flaw, never a virtue.
H1343.portee: Pride is presented in the Bible as one of the worst attitudes of the human heart: it places man in rebellion against God and drives him to oppress the weak. Recognizing this invites the Christian to humility, not to consider themselves superior, and to submit to God. Pride often precedes a fall: those who think they are great will be humbled, while God exalts the humble.

sens: haughty attitude that disregards others and their worth
feeling of superiority that leads to rejecting any advice or correction
pride that manifests in words and behaviors
H1344.detail:
1. Arrogance is the attitude of one who believes themselves superior to others and allows themselves to despise them. It is more than simple personal pride: it is a height that belittles others. In Proverbs 8:13, divine Wisdom proclaims that she hates arrogance just as she hates evil — she places them on the same moral level.
2. Arrogance closes the heart to all correction and advice. One who is afflicted by it refuses to listen because they judge themselves above all judgment. This is why this word appears in a passage where Wisdom enumerates what she abhors.
3. This attitude is revealed through words and actions: "the perverse mouth" that follows in the verse shows how arrogance expresses itself through derogatory or deceitful remarks.
H1344.origine: The Hebrew word גֵּאָה (ge'ah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of lifting, of standing up — the image of a person who raises themselves above others. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting pride and arrogance. This root literally evokes the action of standing upright, but in a moral sense, it designates one who "stands" in an insolent and contemptuous manner.
H1344.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 8:13. It is found in the solemn discourse of Wisdom, which enumerates the attitudes she detests: arrogance is associated with pride, wickedness, and dishonesty. The context shows that arrogance is not simply a personal flaw, but a disposition of the heart that radically opposes the fear of the Lord and the pursuit of wisdom.
H1344.portee: This word reminds the believer that arrogance is incompatible with biblical wisdom and a right relationship with God. It teaches us to cultivate humility, to remain open to correction, and to recognize the worth of others. It is a call to examine our hearts: do we speak and act with hauteur towards those around us?

sens: One of the twelve explorers sent by Moses to scout Canaan
H1345.detail: Gueuel is the name of a man from the tribe of Gad, chosen by Moses as one of the twelve spies tasked with exploring the promised land before Israel's entry into Canaan. His name means "Majesty of God" in Hebrew. He is the son of Maki and appears in the account of the sending of the explorers (Numbers 13:15), where each tribe is represented by a trustworthy man sent to scout the land.
H1345.origine: The name Gueuel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "gé" (majesty, splendor) and "El" (God). This theophoric structure (containing the divine name) was common among the Hebrews, expressing a trust or a quality attributed to God. Gueuel's father, Maki, is mentioned only in this context.
H1345.emploi: Gueuel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:15, during the account where Moses sends twelve explorers ahead to assess the land of Canaan. Each explorer represents their tribe, and Gueuel represents Gad. Unlike Joshua and Caleb, whose faith is highlighted in their report, Gueuel disappears from the narrative after his designation: neither his report nor his reaction to the giants of Canaan is known.
H1345.portee: The choice of Gueuel reminds us that every believer, regardless of their apparent importance in God's story, has a role to play. His name, "Majesty of God", also invites reflection on trusting God in the face of challenges that seem insurmountable: only this divine majesty can provide the courage and faith to enter into God's promises.

sens: Feeling of superiority and exaggerated self-confidence
Haughty attitude of one who despises others
Divine or royal splendor and majesty
Swelling of the waves of the sea
H1346.detail:
1. Pride is primarily an inner feeling of excessive pride and self-sufficiency: the wicked pursues the unfortunate in his pride (Psalms 10:2), convinced of his own importance. It is an inflated self-confidence that distances one from God.
2. This pride manifests externally through a haughty and contemptuous attitude towards others: pride serves as a necklace for the arrogant, violence envelops him like a garment (Psalms 73:6). The arrogant looks down on others and crushes them.
3. The same Hebrew word also denotes the majesty, the grand splendor of God or a king: the God of Israel is carried on high with majesty (Deuteronomy 33:26), expressing the glory that rightfully belongs to Him. Here, it is a legitimate and radiant elevation.
4. Rarely, the word evokes the swelling and surge of the sea, its natural inflation, an image of the powerful movement of water.
H1346.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to rise" or "to swell." The primary image is that of something rising, swelling, taking on volume. In Greek, the same text expresses it with words meaning "pride" or "splendor." The root evokes both natural swelling (like a wave) and the swelling of the human heart that believes itself great.
H1346.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, primarily to denote human pride, particularly that of the wicked or the ungodly nations. In the Psalms and among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zephaniah), pride is denounced as a serious sin, an obstacle to salvation: it brings ruin (Proverbs 29:23). In Moab, pride and arrogance provoke divine judgment (Isaiah 16:6, Jeremiah 48:29). But this same word, in a religious context, also designates the glorious majesty of God or Zion, revealing that elevation becomes sinful when it emanates from the human heart instead of belonging solely to God.
H1346.portee: Pride is presented in the Bible as a root of sin and a rupture with God: the arrogant sets himself up as a rival to God, failing to recognize his dependence. In contrast, seeing in God alone the true majesty and splendor invites the believer to humility and respect. Recognizing that all true greatness comes from God is to be preserved from the fall of the one who is proud.

sens: Greatness, majestic, brilliant excellence
Magnificence, splendor of a thing or being
Haughty pride, arrogance, presumption
Guilty vanity, excessive self-confidence
H1347.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes glorious eminence, imposing greatness: it is the majesty that strikes the eye and inspires respect. When the Bible speaks of the pride (gaon) of God, it evokes His sovereign power and undeniable brilliance — Exodus 15:7 sings: "By the greatness of Your majesty, You overthrow Your adversaries."
2. The same word can describe the magnificence of a city or region: Ezekiel 16:49 reproaches Sodom for its "pride," meaning the magnificent display of its wealth and abundance.
3. But when gaon refers to human pride, it becomes a serious flaw: an inflated pride, excessive pretension that makes man forget his limits and dependence. Isaiah 13:11 announces: "I will put an end to the pride of the haughty."
4. Finally, it is moral vanity, the haughty refusal to acknowledge God or listen to others — the one that Proverbs 16:18 warns against: "Pride goes before destruction." Hosea 5:5 says: "The pride of Israel testifies against him": this people refuses to repent, so great is its arrogance.
H1347.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to rise," "to surge" (like a wave that rises). Gaon primarily denotes what rises, what imposes itself by its height and brilliance: visible majesty. But the image has taken on a moral charge: pride is this height that man wrongly attributes to himself, forgetting that only the majesty of God deserves such brilliance. The word belongs to a rich semantic field: its opposite is lowering, falling (which regularly follows pride in the Bible).
H1347.emploi: This word appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos). It is first used to celebrate divine majesty or that of impressive creatures: God, the swollen Jordan, a great city. But it often describes human pride, that of powerful nations or the ungodly, as an enemy of God. Proverbs ranks it among serious sins. Isaiah and Jeremiah make it a theme of reproach addressed to kings and peoples: their gaon, their guilty self-sufficiency, leads to their downfall. Ezekiel reproaches pride to Sodom and its cities. The word recurs in prophetic threats: God "will bring down the arrogance of tyrants."
H1347.portee: For the believer, this word reminds a fundamental truth: only the majesty of God deserves admiration and respect. Human pride, this self-confidence that forgets God, is a serious sin that always precedes destruction — which is why the Bible consistently warns against it. Recognizing that all true greatness comes from God, not from ourselves, is to enter into the humility that pleases God and protects us from falling.

sens: Excellence, remarkable greatness that inspires respect or admiration
Visible and impressive manifestation of power or presence: column of smoke, swollen waves
Pride, haughty arrogance
Divine splendor and sovereignty of God
H1348.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes imposing greatness, worthy of respect. It is what emanates from an extraordinary presence or act, as when the psalmist celebrates the magnificent things accomplished by God: His action is so great that it deserves to be known throughout the earth (Isaiah 12:5).
2. The word paints a visible and spectacular image: columns of smoke rising from a forest in flames (Isaiah 9:17), or the swollen waves of the sea rising with force (Psalms 89:10). It is what strikes the eye by its physical grandeur.
3. The word also denotes pride, haughty arrogance: one who is filled with majesty in the bad sense does not tolerate an equal. The wicked have haughty words (Psalms 17:10), meaning they swell with pride.
4. When speaking of God, majesty is His splendor and absolute sovereignty. The Lord reigns clothed in majesty (Psalms 93:1): His greatness is not a feeling, but an eternal reality. It is a majesty that commands respect and ignores the pretensions of the wicked (Isaiah 26:10).
H1348.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to rise" or "to be high." Its primary image is that of swelling and elevation: something that rises, swells, and becomes visible — like smoke rising in columns or the sea swelling. This root expresses both what is physically elevated and what surpasses others by its prestige or arrogance. The meaning of "majesty" naturally derives from this: it is what rises above, dominates, and impresses.
H1348.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and Isaiah. It has several uses depending on the context. When referring to God, it denotes His royal splendor and sovereign power: the Lord is clothed in majesty, and it is by it that He maintains the world stable (Psalms 93:1). When speaking of creation, it paints impressive images: the columns of smoke that rise (Isaiah 9:17) or the waves of the sea that God tames (Psalms 89:10). When applied to God's works, it signifies their splendor and greatness (Isaiah 12:5). Finally, when it qualifies man, it becomes negative: it is pride, haughty words, the arrogance of one who refuses to acknowledge God (Psalms 17:10; Isaiah 26:10).
H1348.portee: This word reminds us that true greatness belongs to God alone. It is not vanity, but the splendor of real and just power: it establishes the order of the world and deserves praise (Psalms 93:1; Isaiah 12:5). Conversely, when man adorns himself with a majesty that is not his, it becomes destructive pride, an arrogance that God hates. The believer is called to abandon his own pretension and to contemplate divine majesty to find stability and security.

sens: Exercising the rights of a close relative: reclaiming family property, redeeming a relative sold into slavery, or possibly avenging a murder
Repaying a price to regain possession of something consecrated or sold
Delivering someone from oppression or danger
Restoring someone to lost freedom and dignity
H1350A.detail:
1. In the law of Israel, the kinsman-redeemer (the "redeemer") was the close relative who had the duty and right to take care of family matters: he could buy back the land of a ruined relative (Leviticus 25:25), redeem a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:48), or perpetuate the name of a deceased person by marrying his widow — as Boaz does for Ruth (Ruth 4:1 to 4:8).
2. When someone had dedicated property or an animal to God, he could "redeem" it — that is, take it back — by paying its value plus one-fifth (Leviticus 27:15).
3. For God himself, "redeeming" means delivering his people from oppression: God brings Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 6:6), saves them at the crossing of the Red Sea (Psalms 77:16), and brings them back from exile (Isaiah 52:9).
4. It also means restoring someone's dignity and place: God "redeems Jerusalem," not only by freeing it but by restoring and comforting it (Isaiah 52:9; Isaiah 44:6).
H1350A.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּאַל comes from a root that expresses the idea of "close relative" and "family right." The word reflects a fundamental social institution of Israelite law: the responsibility that a family member has towards others — not out of charity, but out of familial duty. God uses it to describe himself as the Redeemer of Israel, his people — just as a close relative stands as a guarantor for his own.
H1350A.emploi: This verb appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, heavily concentrated in the Law (Leviticus 25 and 27), in the story of Ruth (which beautifully illustrates the institution), and in the prophets, especially Isaiah. In the Law, it describes concrete rights and legal obligations. In the Psalms and among the prophets, God is the subject: he presents himself as the Redeemer of his people in the broadest and deepest sense. The imagery shifts from the legal and familial domain to the spiritual and salvific domain. Job confesses: "I know that my redeemer lives" (Job 19:25), expressing his hope in the midst of suffering.
H1350A.portee: This word reveals that God's salvation is not abstract: he acts as a close relative who has obligations towards his own. In Jesus Christ, God becomes our Redeemer in the ultimate sense — he pays the price for our freedom by shedding his blood. Understanding this word helps the believer see that God does not save us out of distant indifference, but through personal commitment and responsibility of love.

sens: the act of redeeming someone, freeing them by paying a price
liberation of a slave or captive through compensation
deliverance, salvation obtained through divine intervention
H1350B.detail:
1. Redemption refers to the act of reclaiming or liberating someone who is in servitude, slavery, or captivity by paying a price for it. It is an act of purchase for freedom: one pays for someone to be set free. In Isaiah 63:4, the prophet speaks of "the year of my redeemed," referring to the time when God liberates his people from a form of servitude or oppression.
2. The word extends beyond simple economic redemption: it signifies any form of liberation, deliverance from a situation of oppression or danger. In the biblical context, it is often God himself who is the redeemer, intervening to deliver his people from slavery or death.
H1350B.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root גָּאַל (ga'al), which literally means "to free" or "to reclaim." This root evokes the image of a close relative reclaiming what belongs to him by paying the necessary price. In biblical Hebrew, the "redeemer" (go'el) is one who has the right and responsibility to deliver a family member from slavery or death. This notion of redemption through a price is fundamental in biblical thought.
H1350B.emploi: The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 63:4, in a context of judgment and deliverance. The prophet announces a day of vengeance from the Lord, a time when his people will be redeemed, that is, liberated. This passage is part of God's promise to deliver Israel from its enemies and its condition of servitude. Redemption here signifies less a commercial transaction than a salvific intervention from God.
H1350B.portee: Redemption reminds the Christian reader that liberation is never free: it has a cost. This word prepares the heart to understand that God himself pays this price to deliver his people. For the believer, it evokes the regained freedom through the powerful intervention of God, and announces the idea that our salvation was purchased at a great price.

sens: One who avenges the blood of a murdered person by killing the murderer
One who redeems or delivers a family member
One who restores the honor or freedom of a relative
H1350H.detail:
1. The avenger of blood is a family member of a murder victim who has the right, and almost the duty, to kill the murderer to avenge this crime. It is an ancient practice of familial justice: when someone is killed, his close relative becomes his avenger (Numbers 35:19-21). To protect an unintentional murderer, God established cities of refuge where he could escape the wrath of the avenger of blood until his trial (Joshua 20:3, 20:9).
2. More broadly, the avenger is one who intervenes to restore a violated right or redeem a relative: he can redeem a sold family land, free a relative who has fallen into slavery, or perpetuate the name of a deceased man by marrying his widow (as Boaz does for Ruth). This is the role of the "kinsman-redeemer."
3. Figuratively, this term also designates one who intervenes to restore violated order: God himself acts as an avenger by delivering his people from slavery or exile, restoring his justice.
H1350H.origine: The Hebrew verb gaʿal literally means "to remove," "to deliver," or "to bring back to oneself." It comes from a root evoking the action of reappropriating what belongs to the family. The name "avenger" (goʾel) designates one who exercises this right of redemption or deliverance. This word is rich: it speaks of family, debt, and restored honor. Boaz, in the book of Ruth, is a perfect example of the goʾel who redeems land and woman.
H1350H.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Segond, concentrated mainly in the legislative and historical books (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua). Almost all occurrences concern the avenger of blood (goʾel-dam) facing a murderer. The texts of Numbers and Deuteronomy establish the rules: the avenger can only kill if it is a voluntary murder, and the murderer can take refuge in a city of refuge to be judged. The text of 2 Samuel 14:11 shows Joab invoking the law of the avenger of blood before the king. The usage of the word remains legal and familial: it is always a close relative who acts to restore order or the violated family honor.
H1350H.portee: The notion of the avenger of blood reveals how God organized justice in Israel: not through wild vengeance, but through rules that protect the innocent and judge the guilty. The cities of refuge show that God values mercy even in the face of the avenger's wrath. Spiritually, the concept of redemption (beyond vengeance) prepares the reader to understand that Christ is the supreme Redeemer, the one who redeems his people from death and sin.

sens: The closest relative of a person, one who can represent or act on their behalf
One who has the legal right or duty to reclaim what belongs to a family member
H1350I.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the closest relative, one who has rights and responsibilities towards their family. In Numbers 5:8, when a theft cannot be returned to the deceased victim, it is the "relative" (or next of kin) who has the right to receive compensation — it is a family bond that creates a legal responsibility.

2. More broadly, it refers to one who can claim what belongs to their family, particularly to avenge a wrong or reclaim property. In 1 Kings 16:11, the king "did not let anyone who belonged to him escape, neither relative nor friend": he eliminates even close ones, showing that the relative is one who counts by blood and who could have had rights.
H1350I.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּאַל comes from a root that expresses the idea of acting in favor of one's family, protecting one's own. The word encompasses the action of the redeemer or avenger — one who reclaims (redeeming a slave, land, or family reputation). In the Law of Moses, the "redeeming relative" (the goel) is an important legal figure: it is the closest relative who has the duty to redeem a family member who has fallen into slavery or to maintain family lands.
H1350I.emploi: The verb appears in two forms. The Segond translation retains "right" and "relative" for the two occurrences provided, which pertain to legal situations: in Numbers 5:8, the relative (or one who has a right to the inheritance) receives the restitution; in 1 Kings 16:11, the "relative" is listed among those whom the king exterminates. These passages show that the word describes a family relationship with legal consequences — it is one who has the responsibility or right to reclaim a family matter.
H1350I.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, family is not just an emotional relationship: it creates concrete duties and mutual rights. For the believer, it emphasizes the importance of kinship, family solidarity, and respect for legal obligations towards one's own. It is a call to take responsibility for those who are close to us.

sens: To make impure or dirty, to physically soil
To defile by sin or moral evil
To desecrate, to profane what is holy
To exclude from the priesthood due to impurity
H1351.detail:
1. To make impure or dirty, to physically soil: the word primarily refers to the act of covering something with dirt or blood. In Isaiah 63:3, the Lord's garment is soiled with the blood of the enemies He treads in the winepress; in Lamentations 4:14, the priests wander blind in the streets, soiled with blood.

2. To defile by sin or moral evil: the word applies to one who becomes impure through their actions. In Daniel 1:8, Daniel refuses to defile himself by eating the royal foods forbidden by the law; in Isaiah 59:3, the hands of sinners are defiled with blood and crimes.

3. To desecrate, to profane what is holy: to defile means to make an object or place dedicated to God impure or unworthy. Malachi 1:7 speaks of a defiled table offered to the Lord — which profanes worship.

4. To exclude from the priesthood due to impurity: one who is defiled cannot perform priestly functions. In Ezra 2:62 and Nehemiah 7:64, those whose pure genealogy cannot be proven are excluded from the priesthood.
H1351.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of becoming unworthy or impure. It is used particularly for ritual or moral impurity that distances one from the holiness of God. The word belongs to a broad lexical field in Hebrew concerning purity and impurity, which is at the heart of the Law of Moses: one who touches a corpse, transgresses a commandment, or commits evil becomes impure.
H1351.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the books of wisdom and prophecy. The usages cover two areas: on one hand, physical defilement, often blood on clothing or the body (Isaiah 63:3; Lamentations 4:14); on the other hand, moral or ritual defilement, such as that caused by sin (Isaiah 59:3; Daniel 1:8) or by an unworthy offering (Malachi 1:7, 1:12). In the context of the return from exile, the verb is also used to designate exclusion from the priesthood: one whose genealogy cannot be established is barred from divine service (Ezra 2:62; Nehemiah 7:64). The word always carries a nuance of unworthiness or inability to serve God.
H1351.portee: This word reminds us that purity — both ritual and moral — is precious in the eyes of God. For the believer, it invites vigilance over one's actions, thoughts, and intentions in order not to become impure through sin. It is also an exhortation to treat divine worship with respect and sincerity, and not as an empty formality.

sens: Dirt, physical impurity
Moral or religious stain that renders one impure or unworthy
State of what is profaned or corrupted
H1352.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a dirt or impurity that concretely soils something. This is the basic image: something dirty that makes one become impure.
2. Applied to moral and religious life, it describes the stain or dishonor caused by sin or transgression. In Nehemiah 13:29, Nehemiah prays to God to remember those who have "defiled the priesthood" — meaning they have committed acts that tarnished the purity required for the service of God and violated the covenant of the priesthood.
3. It is also the state of what has been profaned or corrupted, becoming unworthy of its role or consecration.
H1352.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of dirt and defilement, very common in the Law of Moses to describe states of ritual or moral impurity. This root always evokes degradation, an affront to purity.
H1352.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in Nehemiah 13:29, in the context of the temple reform after the exile. Nehemiah denounces those who have mixed races or committed acts that violated the covenant of the priesthood and the purity of worship. The term underscores the seriousness of these infractions: it is not just about faults, but about active contamination of what is sacred.
H1352.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin is never trivial: it defiles, it stains what is holy. For the Christian, it invites serious consideration of the issue of moral purity and holiness, not as a set of external rules, but as the preservation of a right relationship with God. It is an invitation to vigilance and repentance.

sens: Action of redeeming something, recovering it by paying
Legal right of a person to redeem a sold property
Price paid for this recovery
Kinship obligation that compels this recovery
Set of relatives, kinship
H1353.detail:
1. Redemption is the act of regaining possession of a property (a land, a house, or even a person) by paying a price. It is a buy-back: the one who sold can recover what he has ceded if he has the means (Leviticus 25:51).

2. The right of redemption is the legal prerogative recognized for someone to reclaim a property. The law of Israel grants this right first to the original owner, then to his close relatives: "If there are still many years, he shall pay his redemption according to the price of those years" (Leviticus 25:48).

3. Redemption also refers to the price itself, the sum of money required for this recovery (Leviticus 25:51).

4. Finally, it is a link: the one who has the right of redemption is a close relative, a redeemer, someone from the family obligated by kinship to intervene (Ruth 4:6).

5. The term can also refer to kinship itself, the set of family ties that create this obligation of redemption.
H1353.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to deliver, to take away, to recover." It denotes the action of taking something away from someone else to return it to the one who once possessed it. The Greek of the Old Testament translates this word as "lytron" (price of ransom, price of redemption) or "agorazo" (to buy, to acquire). The biblical notion of redemption is based on the principle that all property ultimately belongs to God, and that everyone has the right to reclaim it according to their position in the family.
H1353.emploi: This word appears 13 times, almost exclusively in legal texts (Leviticus 25) and in narratives that apply these laws (Ruth, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It governs a very concrete legal system: an Israelite who sells his land or house can redeem it (Leviticus 25:24 and 29), and if he himself is sold as a slave, his relatives are obligated to redeem him by paying the price (Leviticus 25:48). The "goel," the redeemer, is the close relative who exercises this right. In Leviticus 25:32, the Levites have a "perpetual right of redemption" of their houses. Ruth 4:6 shows a case where the one who had this right gives it up to another, reminding us that it is a privilege tied to kinship. The word illustrates the economic and social order of Israel: properties are not permanently alienated, and blood ties impose mutual duties.
H1353.portee: Redemption, as the Bible presents it, reveals a theology: no one is abandoned, no property escapes forever from the one who had it. There is always the possibility of restoration and recovery when one has the means and a right. This law protects the poor and values family ties as a force of solidarity. For the Christian, these practices also foreshadow the idea that sinful humanity can be redeemed, recovered by God — a theme that will become central in the New Testament with the work of Christ, the ultimate "redeemer."

sens: Convex surface, bulging of something
Back of the human body
Eyebrow or brow ridge
Rim or circumference of a wheel
Bulging projection of a shield
Fortification or entrenchment (figuratively)
H1354.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a convex or bulging surface — any part that protrudes. This is the most general image: something that has relief, roundness (Ezekiel 1:18 speaks of the "terrifying circumference" of the wheels, this bulge that surrounds them).
2. On the human body, it refers to the back — the surface of the body between the shoulders and the loins. In Psalms 129:3, we see the plowmen tracing furrows on the back, an image of the torture or suffering inflicted on the people of God.
3. The word also applies to the eyebrow or brow ridge (Leviticus 14:9: shaving the eyebrow is part of ritual purification).
4. It can denote the rim or edge of a wheel — its rim that goes around (1 Kings 7:33 lists the parts of the wheels of the Temple: axles, rims, spokes, hubs).
5. On a shield, it refers to the central bulge or relief (Job 15:26: running toward God "under the thick back of the shields" means advancing protected by these massive projections).
6. Figuratively, the word can denote fortifications or entrenchments of a defense — the arguments one raises (Job 13:12: the words of his friends are "entrenchments of mud," meaning fragile and unfounded).
H1354.origine: The Hebrew word גַּב (gav) fundamentally means "that which curves, that which rises." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of bulging or relief. The same root appears in other forms with related meanings: גִּבְעָה (gibéa, "hill"), גּוֹבַה (gouba, "height"). The word always describes something that protrudes or rises above the flat.
H1354.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe concrete realities. In the laws of purity (Leviticus 14:9), it refers to the eyebrow that must be shaved. In the description of the Temple's constructions (1 Kings 7:33, Ezekiel), it refers to mechanical elements: axles, circumferences of wheels. In poetry (Psalms 129:3, Job 15:26), it becomes the image of the suffering body, of inflicted torture or of warrior protection. In Ezekiel, it also depicts illicit high places and the fortifications of idols. The meaning varies according to the context: always a bulging surface or a protrusion, but applied to very diverse realities — anatomical, architectural, or martial.
H1354.portee: This word reminds us that the human body is the object of God's attention — even down to details like the eyebrow. It also emphasizes how our sufferings are visible and known ("he has traced long furrows on my back"). In the background, the image of the "thick back of the shields" evokes divine protection: God is our "back," the one on whom we lean to face the enemy. Finally, the image of unfounded entrenchments warns us that our personal defenses — our arguments, our justifications — are as fragile as mud if they do not rest on God.

sens: the posterior part of the body, between the shoulders and the loins
side, flank of something
edge, rim, ridge of a surface
H1355.detail:
1. The back is the rear part of the human or animal body, from the neck to the loins. This is the most natural image of the Hebrew word gav.
2. By extension, gav denotes the side or flank of an object — its lateral face. In Aramaic (the language spoken in Babylon), the word can also evoke the edge, lip, or ridge of a surface.
3. In Daniel 7:6, the leopard has "four wings of a bird on its back": the back becomes the flat surface where the wings unfold, an image of a winged creature.
H1355.origine: Gav comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of "that which rises" or "that which protrudes." In Hebrew, it is a simple masculine noun. Aramaic, a closely related language used in the last biblical books, shares this word with a broader range of meanings: back, edge, rim, ridge. This linguistic proximity reflects the belonging of both languages to the same Semitic family.
H1355.emploi: Gav appears very rarely in the Hebrew Bible — a single occurrence in Aramaic, in Daniel 7:6. This passage describes a prophetic vision where God shows Daniel four monstrous beasts rising from the sea. The third beast, resembling a leopard, has four wings of a bird on its back. The image of the back serves here as a surface where the hybrid and superhuman nature of the creature is inscribed: its wings express both its power and its strange character. The prophetic context gives the word a symbolic charge: the back is no longer merely anatomical, but the place where signs of supernatural power are displayed.
H1355.portee: This word reminds us that even the apocalyptic visions of Daniel are expressed in images of the body. The back of the visionary leopard invites the reader to see how God paints the future with the forms of the created world — here, the contrast between a terrestrial animal and celestial wings. It is an invitation to read biblical symbols not as abstract riddles, but as living images that speak to our imagination.

sens: Excavation creusée dans le sol pour recueillir l'eau
Trou ou tranchée destiné à d'autres usages pratiques
H1356A.detail:
1. A pit is primarily a hollow dug intentionally in the ground to store rainwater or spring water: it is a cistern. In 2 Kings 3:16, the prophet instructs the king to dig pits in a valley to collect the water that God will send. It is an essential installation in dry land, and when these pits are empty, as in Jeremiah 14:3, it is a sign of terrible drought.
2. More broadly, a pit can be any hollow in the ground: a trench, a depression, an excavation dug for other reasons, not just for water. The word refers to the hole itself, whether it is intended to hold water or serve another practical function.
H1356A.origine: The Hebrew word gev comes from a root evoking the idea of hollow, void, of something that sinks. It is related to the vital necessity of water in the land of Canaan, where rain is rare and concentrated in winter: digging pits or cisterns was essential for survival. The word has retained this concrete image of a dug hole.
H1356A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Kings 3:16, it refers to pits to be dug in a valley to accumulate the rainwater that God is about to send miraculously; it is an act of faith by the king who prepares to receive the blessing. In Jeremiah 14:3, these same pits (rendered as 'cisterns') are empty during a drought, an image of God's abandonment; the little servants go there to seek water and return ashamed and confused for finding none. In both cases, the pit embodies the people's dependence on the elements and on God's will.
H1356A.portee: The pit reminds us that survival depends on God and the wisdom of preparing to receive His gifts. In 2 Kings, digging the pits is acting in faith while awaiting divine help. In Jeremiah, the empty cisterns symbolize the absence of God and the despair of the people without His aid. This humble word speaks of our vulnerability and our constant need to depend on God's grace.

sens: Site of battles between David and the Philistines
Another name for Gezer
H1359.detail:
1. Gob is a place where at least two military encounters took place between David's forces and the Philistines. It is where Sibbecai defeated Saph, one of the giants from the family of Rapha (2 Samuel 21:18), and where Elhanan defeated Goliath of Gath (2 Samuel 21:19). This name can mean "cistern" or "pit," which could evoke a rugged terrain or a geographically significant location.
2. Gob is another designation for Gezer, an important city in Canaan. The two names likely refer to the same place or region, although textual traditions vary among manuscripts.
H1359.origine: The Hebrew word גֹּב (gov) literally means "cistern" or "pit," which evokes an excavation or hollow in the ground. It belongs to a family of words describing cavities or reservoirs. The name can also be linked to Gezer (גֶּזֶר), a well-known city in the territory of Canaan. Ancient traditions sometimes considered Gob and Gezer as two names for the same location.
H1359.emploi: Gob appears twice in the biblical text, exclusively in 2 Samuel 21, in verses 18 and 19. These two verses describe battles between David's warriors and the Philistines at the same location. In the first passage, it is the site of Sibbecai's victory over the giant Saph; in the second, it is where Elhanan defeated Goliath. These accounts are part of a series of fights against Philistine giants and show that this place was a strategic or frequent point of conflict between Israel and its enemies.

sens: Underground reservoir dug into rock or built of masonry to collect and store rainwater
Stagnant body of water, marsh, or wetland
Figuratively: place of storage or reserve
H1360.detail: 1. A cistern is a reservoir dug or built to collect and hold water, essential in the dry regions of the Middle East where water is precious. In Isaiah 30:14, the cistern is mentioned as a useful everyday object: water is drawn from it for domestic needs, highlighting its practical importance in ancient life. 2. The word also refers to wetlands, marshes, or stagnant bodies of water that cannot be drained or cultivated. In Ezekiel 47:11, the marshes and pits remain unclean and useless, unlike the living waters of the river that heal the land. 3. Figuratively, a cistern can represent a place of reserve or conservation, as when the psalmist speaks of the heart that retains precious words.
H1360.origine: The Hebrew word גֶּ֫בֶא (ge.ve) comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or hollowing out a cavity. It belongs to a family of words describing containers and pits. The cistern was an ancient and essential invention in Egypt and the Levant for surviving periods of drought.
H1360.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 30:14, it refers to an ordinary cistern, a fragile object of daily life used for drawing water. In Ezekiel 47:11, the same Hebrew term (translated as marsh) describes swampy areas that, unlike the life-giving waters of the river, remain unproductive and without blessing. Both uses show the word associated with water, either stored usefully or stagnant and useless.
H1360.portee: The cistern reminds us that water is a blessing from God, to be preserved and used wisely. It also symbolizes how our hearts can retain what is precious to us — the Word of God or divine protection. But it also warns: a reserve that runs dry or stagnant water loses its value. This invites the believer to seek the living waters of the Spirit rather than drying sources.

sens: To be high, to have great size or height
To rise, to go upward
To be exalted, to have dignity or honor
To be proud, to have a heart swollen with pride
H1361.detail:
1. The primary and physical meaning is simply "to be high": to have great size or stature. When Saul stands before the people, he "towers" over them all by a head (1 Samuel 10:23), meaning he is physically taller.

2. The verb also means "to rise" in the sense of ascending, going up in position or altitude. The heavens and the clouds are "above" man (Job 35:5); the servant of the Lord "will be lifted very high" (Isaiah 52:13).

3. On a moral and spiritual level, "to rise" means to be elevated in dignity, to be honored, to be exalted. God "lifts up" the tree that was low (Ezekiel 17:24): He causes it to grow by promoting it.

4. In a negative sense, "to rise" means to become proud, to swell with pride: the heart rises because of beauty or success (Ezekiel 28:17). It is the same physical image (the heart that rises), but now expresses arrogance and refusal to recognize one's smallness before God.
H1361.origine: The Hebrew root "gavah" fundamentally means "to be high, to rise." It evokes the image of a person or thing growing in height. The verb can be used literally (size, stature) or figuratively (honor, dignity, or pride). This image of "high" and "low" runs throughout the Bible to speak of dignity, power, and humility.
H1361.emploi: The verb "gavah" appears 33 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs), the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah), and the Psalms. Its meaning varies: literally, it describes great height (1 Samuel 10:23) or the altitude of the clouds (Job 35:5). Figuratively positively, it speaks of God's exaltation (Psalms 113:5) or His servant's (Isaiah 52:13). In a frequently negative figurative sense, it denounces pride: the heart that rises with pride (Ezekiel 28:17, 2 Chronicles 26:16), the haughty eyes of the daughters of Zion (Isaiah 3:16), or the arrogance that precedes a fall (Proverbs 18:12). The contrast between rising before God and rising against God structures many of these uses.
H1361.portee: This word reminds the believer of the crucial difference between two forms of elevation: rising in dignity before God when one obeys and follows Him, or rising in pride when one rebels against Him. Humility — not allowing one's heart to swell with pride — is true greatness. It is a lesson in balance: God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud.

sens: Vertical distance, dimension of an object from bottom to top
Elevation, high position in space or social status
Greatness, magnificence, splendor
Pride, arrogance, excessive self-esteem
H1363.detail:
1. Height is primarily a measurable, physical dimension: the height of a man (1 Samuel 17:4: Goliath is six cubits tall), the dimension of a building (2 Chronicles 3:4), that of a tree or plant (Ezekiel 19:11: the tree dominates "by its height").
2. It then denotes a high position: being above, at the top (Job 22:12: "Is not God on high in the heavens?"). It also refers to the moral or social elevation of a person or nation.
3. Height can signify greatness, magnificence, splendor — that which impresses by its magnitude or prestige (Ezekiel 31:10: the tree boasted "of its height").
4. Finally, height often becomes arrogance, excessive pride: the pride of the heart that rises against God (Psalms 10:4: the wicked says "with arrogance"; Jeremiah 48:29: the pride of Moab, its "height", its arrogance). It is the exaltation of self that leads to a fall.
H1363.origine: The Hebrew word גֹּבַהּ (govah) comes from the root גָּבַהּ (gavah), which means "to be high, to rise up". The same root produces related words: גָּבוֹהַ (gavôah, "high"), and it expresses the physical and then moral idea of elevation. In the Bible, this upward movement is loaded with meaning: physical elevation can become elevation of pride, and the Bible warns against this confusion.
H1363.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books (Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in history (Samuel, Chronicles). The usages vary according to context: in 1 Samuel 17:4, it refers to Goliath's physical height; in 2 Chronicles 3:4, it is the dimension of the Temple; in Job 22:12, it is God's position in the heavens. But the moral sense predominates: very often, "height" refers to pride (Psalms 10:4, Jeremiah 48:29, Proverbs 16:18). Ezekiel exploits this ambiguity: the magnificent tree boasted of its height before falling, an image of pride that precedes ruin.
H1363.portee: This word teaches that elevation, whether physical, social, or spiritual, hides a trap: the temptation to become proud. The Bible does not condemn greatness in itself, but the arrogance that follows. For the believer, the word reminds us that only God truly remains "on high" (Job 22:12), and that all human height must humble itself before Him. Thus, Hezekiah "humbled himself" and found grace (2 Chronicles 32:26).

sens: Of great height or elevation in space
Located high up, away from the ground or ordinary level
Exceeding the norm, intense or considerable
Proud, full of arrogance
Having importance, dignity (in a moral or social sense)
H1364.detail:
1. The word first describes what physically rises above the ground — the high mountains covered by the waters of the flood (Genesis 7:19), or a tall man like Saul (1 Samuel 9:2). The image is one of verticality.

2. It then qualifies what is situated at a height: the high places where altars are built (1 Kings 14:23), the high mountains where wild animals take refuge (Psalms 104:18), or the tall towers of fortified cities (Isaiah 2:15). The elevated place dominates the landscape.

3. The word can also express amplitude or intensity: the Leviathan inspires such deep and great fear that one can say everything is "high" (Job 41:25).

4. In a moral sense, "high" becomes "haughty" or "proud": one who has a proud heart and looks down on others (Psalms 101:5, Proverbs 16:5). Pride manifests itself in lifting the head.

5. Finally, the word carries a nuance of dignity and power: what is elevated commands, dominates — whether it is a social position (Ezekiel 21:31, where what is brought low will be raised and what is high will be brought low) or divine majesty.
H1364.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that literally means "to become great" or "to rise up". It evokes the image of ascending, gaining height. This same root is found in related words that express greatness, exaltation, pride. Ancient Hebrew naturally saw physical height as an image of strength, power, and importance: what is high is not easily accessible, controls what is below, and inspires respect or fear.
H1364.emploi: This word appears approximately 36 times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes geographical realities: mountains, towers, buildings. But very early on, it shifts towards moral and religious meaning. The "high places" (elevated hills with altars) regularly appear in the history of Israel (1 Kings 14:23, Jeremiah 2:20, 2 Kings 17:10) as traps of idolatry. The word also applies to human pride: God "brings down" the haughty looks (1 Samuel 2:3) and resists those with an elevated heart (Proverbs 16:5). Finally, it sometimes qualifies what is impressive or grand: the Leviathan inspires great fear, Pharaoh's stature evokes admiration. Ezekiel uses the word to depict the final reversal: what was exalted is brought low, what was humbled is raised (Ezekiel 21:31, Isaiah 5:15).
H1364.portee: This word reveals the logic of divine judgment: God sees the heart, not the appearance, and He brings down precisely what is lifted up in pride. For the believer, "high" becomes a warning against pride and a call to humility: the haughty remain far from God, while the one who humbles himself tastes His favor (Isaiah 57:15: "I dwell near the humble and contrite"). The word also invites us to contemplate the inviolable majesty of God, which surpasses all earthly heights.

sens: Arrogance and contempt, disdainful look directed at others
Excessive pride that leads someone to believe they are superior
State of insolence before God
H1365.detail:
1. This word denotes haughty pride, that attitude of arrogance where one looks down on others. Isaiah 2:11 speaks of "the man with a haughty look": this is one who, filled with his own importance, allows himself to despise others.
2. It is also excessive pride, the character of one who believes themselves superior and refuses to submit. The text in Isaiah 2:17 contrasts this "haughty" one who "will be brought low" with the Lord alone who "will be exalted".
3. Ultimately, this height of pride is an attitude of insolence before God, an implicit refusal to recognize one's place as a creature. It directly offends the Lord who alone deserves glory.
H1365.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "elevated" or "high". The height of pride is thus concretely the attitude of one who stands up, who elevates themselves — a physical image of a posture of arrogance. It is the opposite of humility, which means to lower oneself and recognize one's smallness before God.
H1365.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the prophet Isaiah, a few verses apart. In Isaiah 2:11 and 2:17, Isaiah announces the day when the Lord will judge and bring down all those who are "haughty" — that is, the men who have risen in pride. These two passages are part of a prophecy of eschatological judgment: the day of the Lord will consume human pride, and God alone will be exalted. The use of the word is therefore always negative and prophetic.
H1365.portee: This word warns us against spiritual pride — the tendency to believe ourselves important, strong, or right by ourselves. Whenever we rise in arrogance, we imitate the attitude that God promises to bring low. Scripture invites us to cultivate humility, this recognition that we are small and that glory belongs to God alone. It is a call to guard against pride before God humbles us.

sens: Line or point that marks the separation between two territories or domains
Defined and delimited territorial space, region
Boundary or concrete marker indicating a border
Extent, measurable dimension of a space
End, extremity of an extent
H1366G.detail:
1. A limit is a demarcation line between two regions — like the border that separates two kingdoms or two inheritances. Exodus 23:31 describes the limits that God establishes for Israel: "from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river." 
2. The word also refers to the territory itself, the delimited region. Numbers 35:27 speaks of the "territory of the city of refuge": this is the protected space assigned to a city.
3. A limit can be marked by a physical boundary, such as an edge or ridge (Ezekiel 43:13: the "edge" of the altar). It is then the visible object that shows how far something extends.
4. The word also expresses the idea of dimension or measurable extent: a land has its limits, its boundaries that define its size.
5. Figuratively, "limit" can mean the extremity or end of a domain: reaching the limit means arriving at its term.
H1366G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to enclose" or "to circumscribe." It conveys the idea of drawing a line, tracing a contour to define a space. Words from the same family express the idea of division, separation, and circumscription. This root appears in several Hebrew words that talk about territorial divisions and delimitations.
H1366G.emploi: This word appears 115 times in the Bible, mainly in historical and legislative books (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua). It is common in descriptions of the territories of the tribes of Israel (notably Joshua 13-19), cities of refuge, and royal possessions. The word is also used for the borders of neighboring peoples (Moab, Ammon) and the promised lands. Sometimes, it simply designates a boundary or spatial marker (Ezekiel 43:13). The Segond also translates the word as "side" when referring to the sides of a region (Joshua 15:5: "eastern limit").
H1366G.portee: Understanding that God establishes limits helps the believer grasp that order and delimitation come from God — it is not by chance that a land has its boundaries. The concept of limit also reminds us that everyone has their assigned part and must respect it. Finally, when we read that God "establishes limits" (Exodus 23:31), it shows that divine providence reigns over space and history.

sens: Line or area that marks the separation between two regions, two properties, or two peoples
Region, country, or expanse of land subject to the authority of a people or a king
Defined and delimited area, zone of influence or action
Space, extent (in a figurative sense, like the region of darkness)
H1366H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the line or area that separates two spaces: the border between two peoples, as in Deuteronomy 2:4 where the people of Israel must pass "at the border of your brothers, the children of Esau." It is a drawn and recognizable limit.
2. It also refers to the territory itself, that is, the region that a people inhabits and possesses. When Judges 11:22 says that the Israelites "took possession of all the territory of the Amorites," it speaks of the entire land they occupied between two rivers. It is the defined extent of a possession.
3. The word can also describe a particular area or domain of action. In Ezekiel 48, it involves tracing the portions of land that each tribe will inhabit in the restored land: each tribe will have its own clearly delimited territory.
4. Rarely, it is used figuratively to designate a sphere or abstract domain, as in Job 38:20 where God speaks of "the region of darkness."
H1366H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of delimitation, of drawing a line. It is related to the verb "gabal" which means "to trace a limit." The central notion is that of a region clearly delimited by its natural or conventional borders. This term is also used in administrative and geographical texts to describe the portions of land distributed or possessed.
H1366H.emploi: The word appears about 85 times in the Old Testament, particularly in historical books and among the prophets. It is very frequent in the book of Joshua, where it describes how the promised land is divided among the tribes of Israel: each tribe receives its territory with precise limits (Joshua 16:3, 19:10, 19:18, etc.). It also appears in accounts of military conquests: David and his successors "extend" their territory, meaning they enlarge their borders (2 Kings 18:8). The word is used for natural borders (rivers, mountains) and political borders between neighboring peoples. Among the prophets, it can designate threatened or restored territories.
H1366H.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how God organizes the sharing of the promised land among the tribes of Israel, and how borders mark the identity and independence of peoples. It is a reminder that God distributes lands with order and justice, giving each their delimited share. For the Christian faith, this also evokes how God establishes limits in His creation and in His governance of nations.

sens: line or point that marks the end of a territory, region
extent of a territory, its contours and borders
border zone, boundary region
delimited space assigned to someone
H1367.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the line that traces the outline of a country or property: the Jordan forms the eastern limit of the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 18:20), or it is a fixed line that must not be crossed.
2. It applies to all the contours that define a territory: God gives Israel "the land of Canaan, of which here are the limits" (Numbers 34:2), and He sets "the limits of the peoples" according to the number of the children of Israel (Deuteronomy 32:8).
3. The word can also evoke the border region itself, the space that borders a territory and marks its confines.
4. Finally, it designates the space assigned to someone, their lot or portion: each tribe receives its possession "with its limits" defined on all sides (Joshua 19:49).
H1367.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to surround" or "to gird," evoking the idea of tracing a line around something to delimit it. It belongs to the same family as other words concerning borders and separations. The underlying image is that of a tracing that separates, that "girds" a space and makes it distinct from its environment.
H1367.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and law books (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua). Its primary use is geographical: defining the borders of tribal territories during the division of Canaan, or the boundaries of kingdoms (Numbers 32:33, 34:2, 34:12; Joshua 18:20, 19:49). It is also used in a broader sense of "domain" or "kingdom," when speaking of the limits that God sets for nations and peoples (Deuteronomy 32:8). The context is always that of territorial organization and divine allocation of spaces.
H1367.portee: This word reminds us that God organizes history and geography according to His sovereign design: He assigns to each people, to each tribe its place and its borders. For the Christian reader, this evokes the idea that our lives also have their limits, set by God's will, and that these limits are not a punishment but a benevolent organization of our inheritance in Christ.

sens: Strong man, capable and courageous in battle
Valiant warrior, elite soldier
Powerful or influential person in a field
Heroic figure, famous character
H1368.detail:
1. A valiant person is primarily one who possesses physical strength and courage to fight. He is a capable and feared warrior: David is surrounded by valiant men who follow him into battle (2 Samuel 23:8-9), and the king of Judah raises valiant men to form his army (2 Chronicles 17:14).

2. The term also designates a warrior recognized for his proven valor in battle, one who stands out through his exploits. The valiant of Moab lose courage like a woman in labor before the threat (Jeremiah 48:41), so great was their reputation for strength.

3. More broadly, a valiant person can be a man of power and influence, strong in his field—not just military. Naaman, a powerful general of the king of Syria, is called a valiant man despite his leprosy, because he dominates by his authority (2 Kings 5:1).

4. The word can also qualify a person or a figure who has become legendary, a famous hero. Thus, the giants born of the union of the sons of God and the daughters of men are called heroes, having become famous in antiquity (Genesis 6:4).
H1368.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses strength, power, and capability. It is related to other terms of physical and moral strength. The basic image is one of robustness, muscle, and resilience. In the Bible, the word has taken on nuances of honor and reputation: a valiant person is not only strong, he is recognized as such and feared.
H1368.emploi: The word appears about 152 times in the Old Testament, mainly in war narratives and in the genealogies of warriors. It is very frequent in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), less so in others. David is surrounded by valiant men who form his elite army (2 Samuel 23); the kings of Judah count their valiant men to assess their military power (2 Chronicles 17:14). In the funeral poems about Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1), the valiant are celebrated for their exploits. The term always carries a shade of admiration or respect.
H1368.portee: This word reminds us that God recognizes and values courage, moral strength, and the ability to overcome obstacles. It invites the reader to contemplate the valiant of God's people—not to imitate a warrior's brutality, but to learn how trust in God produces true courage. David himself, the greatest valiant of the people, draws his strength from his covenant with the Lord, not from his mere musculature.

sens: Physical strength, vigor of the body or an army
Warrior value, bravery in battle
Powerful acts, accomplished exploits
Ability to exercise authority, domination
Divine power, sovereign strength of God
