H1369.detail:
1. Power is primarily raw strength—that of a robust man, of a well-organized army. Exodus 32:18 speaks of the cry of the defeated and the victors: this is physical power, the capacity to conquer.
2. It also designates bravery in battle, the moral vigor of the warrior who does not flee (Job 39:22 speaks of the horse that fears nothing). It is the strength of character that allows one to stand firm.
3. This word applies to concrete acts, memorable exploits: 2 Kings 13:12 enumerates the "exploits" of the kings of Israel, the wars, the constructions—everything that shows that a king has counted.
4. Power can also mean authority, the right to command and govern. He who has power imposes his will.
5. Finally, and this is crucial in the Bible, power belongs sovereignly to God. Psalms 150:2 asks us to praise God for "his mighty acts," and Job 12:13 affirms that "power" resides in God alone—a force that creates, judges, saves, and transforms.
H1369.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be strong, to prevail." The corresponding verb is very active in the Bible to describe one who conquers or dominates. In Aramaic, the word has the same form and meaning. This power is never abstract: it always manifests itself through concrete acts—a raised arm, an army on the march, a miracle. That is why the Bible rarely speaks of power without immediately mentioning what it does.
H1369.emploi: The word appears 61 times in the Old Testament. The kings of Israel and Judah possess it, and their "exploits" are enumerated in the royal chronicles (2 Kings 13:12, 14:15, 14:28, 20:20). Warriors and peoples manifest it in battle (Judges 5:31, Judges 8:21). But the most frequent and theological use concerns the power of God: it is praised in the Psalms (71:18, 145:4, 150:2), it dominates the powers of nature (Psalms 65:7), it accomplishes wonderful acts (Jeremiah 16:21). Isaiah 30:15 contrasts human power with trust in God—a significant moral nuance: power only saves if it comes from God.
H1369.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God alone truly holds power—not money, nor weapons, nor cunning. Recognizing God's power means accepting that he governs history and can transform our darkest circumstances. This word also invites us to seek our strength not in ourselves, but in reliance on God, as Isaiah 30:15 asks. Finally, it exhorts us to praise the exploits of God, visible in creation and in redemption.

sens: power, ability to accomplish great things
vigor, energy deployed to overcome resistance
domination, authority exercised over others or over events
H1370.detail:
1. "Strength" is primarily effective power: the concrete ability to do, to act, to accomplish what seems impossible. In Daniel 2:23, the prophet praises God because he has given him this strength capable of revealing the hidden secrets of the king.
2. It is also vigor, the energy that allows one to overcome an obstacle or resistance. It implies real action, deployed to overcome a difficulty.
3. It also designates the power, the authority by which one dominates or commands. When it is said that strength belongs to God (Daniel 2:20), it affirms that he alone has supreme authority and power over all things.
H1370.origine: The Hebrew word gu'bourah (גְּבוּרָה) comes from the root gabar (גבר), which means "to be strong" or "to prevail." It evokes the image of a power that acts, triumphs, and imposes itself. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms describing virile strength, warrior or divine energy. The form here is Aramaic, used in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.
H1370.emploi: This word appears twice in the book of Daniel, in verses 20 and 23 of chapter 2, both spoken by the prophet himself. In both cases, it is about glorifying God for his strength: a strength that includes wisdom (the ability to know and reveal secrets) and the power to act. God's "strength" is not blind brutality, but a power united with wisdom, capable of revealing and accomplishing the divine purpose.
H1370.portee: Understanding that God possesses true strength is not a theological abstraction: it is recognizing that he can really act in history, truly transform situations, and truly keep his promises. For the believer, turning to this strength of God is to trust in someone who has the real power to accomplish what he says.

sens: Who has lost their hair, particularly on the forehead or the top of the head
H1371.detail: 1. The word refers to a person devoid of hair, especially on the front of the skull. In the context of the purity laws in Leviticus, the text specifies that a person who is "bald in front" — that is, who has lost their hair on the forehead — is pure, unlike other physical conditions that may render someone impure according to Mosaic law (Leviticus 13:41).
H1371.origine: The Hebrew word gibbeach comes from a root that evokes the idea of a bare or exposed surface, particularly the forehead or the top of the head. It is a simple descriptive term that paints a concrete image of the absence of hair.
H1371.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 13:41, in the context of laws regarding defects and skin diseases that affect ritual purity. The passage distinguishes between different forms of baldness, establishing that this condition, in itself, does not render someone impure before God — an important nuance to show that Mosaic law does not prohibit a simple natural physical condition.
H1371.portee: This biblical mention reminds us that visible physical defects do not exclude one from the community of God's people. It emphasizes that ritual purity in the Old Testament did not depend on outward appearance, but on specific conditions defined by the law, inviting the reader to look beyond appearances.

sens: Region of the skull devoid of hair, either naturally (due to age) or pathologically (due to a disease)
Area stripped of fabric, worn or frayed
Absence, lack, void
H1372.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the bald area of the human skull — either the top of the head or the forehead. In Leviticus 13:42-43, the priest must examine whether a whitish sore appears on this bald region: it is a possible sign of leprosy. The image is that of a bare skull, visible, without the protection of hair.
2. In Leviticus 13:55, the term applies to a worn fabric, stripped of its fibers: "the reverse" or the worn part of a cloth, which has lost its protective layer. The meaning shifts from the body to clothing, by analogy — a bare, defective surface.
3. More abstractly, the word can evoke the idea of absence, nudity, of what is lacking or has gone away.
H1372.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of bare, stripped. It is related to the concept of nudity or lack of covering. The form primarily exists in cultic or diagnostic contexts, particularly in the purity laws of Leviticus, where any visible defect of the body or clothing has ritual significance.
H1372.emploi: The word appears only three times in Leviticus 13, in the code of impurities. It is found in the ritual medical examination of lepers: the priest must distinguish between simple baldness (natural, thus pure) and leprosy that may manifest (impure). Its use in 13:55 applies it to a worn fabric, showing that "bald spot" also designates any bare area, regardless of the object. The context is strictly legal and diagnostic — no figurative meaning.
H1372.portee: This word reminds the believer that the law of Moses was attentive to the concrete life of the people and carefully distinguished the natural from the pathological, the pure from the impure. It illustrates God's love for order and holiness, even in the details of daily life. For today's physician or caregiver, this passage shows that careful observation and responsible diagnosis have always mattered in God's covenant with His people.

sens: Leader of a Benjamite family in Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H1373.detail: Gabbai is a man who lived during the time of exile and return, mentioned only once in the Bible. His name appears in the list of leaders of Benjamite families settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile, alongside Sallai and others. He represents one of the important families that participated in the reconstruction of the religious and civil life of Jerusalem.
H1373.origine: His name, Gabbai, literally means "my back" or "behind me" in Hebrew. Although the etymology is simple, its exact meaning remains unclear: it may evoke a position or quality, but the biblical text tells us nothing more. Gabbai is a simple proper name, with no verbal root exploited elsewhere in Scripture.
H1373.emploi: Gabbai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:8. He appears in the genealogical list of leaders of Benjamite families who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (around 445 B.C.). This list, part of the book of Nehemiah dedicated to the repopulation of the city, shows that his family was significant enough to be named among the prominent families.

sens: Village north of Jerusalem, located between Anathoth and Nob
H1374.detail: Geba is a small village located north of Jerusalem, between the towns of Anathoth and Nob. The name literally means "cisterns" in Hebrew, which likely evokes the rocky geography of this place where water reservoirs were dug. The only known biblical usage shows its inhabitants fleeing during the advance of the Assyrian army toward Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:31).
H1374.origine: The name Geba comes from the Hebrew "gob" which means "cistern" or "pit." The plural "geba" thus designates cisterns, suggesting that this village was characterized by its water reservoirs dug into the rock, a common practice in Judea to conserve water during dry periods.
H1374.emploi: Geba appears only once in the Bible, in the description of the route of the Assyrian army approaching Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah enumerates the towns and villages in the north that are terrified by this military advance: Madmena disperses and the inhabitants of Geba flee. This passage illustrates how the Assyrian invasion sowed panic among the small localities of Judea before reaching the capital.

sens: Drinking vessel, usually made of metal or ceramic
Calice-shaped part of a candlestick or ornamental object
What one drinks, metaphorically the fate or will of God
H1375.detail:
1. A cup is a vessel intended to hold and drink a liquid. In Genesis 44, Joseph hides his silver cup in Benjamin's sack to detain him: it is a valuable object, a personal and domestic possession that one would not want to lose without shame.
2. The candlestick of the sanctuary, described in Exodus 25, is adorned with small cups shaped like almonds — floral elements that complement the main stem and its branches. These cups are ornamental carvings in gold, not functional vessels.
3. By extension, the cup metaphorically designates what one must drink, that is, experience or accept. When Joseph says that whoever has the cup will be his slave, he is no longer just talking about a stolen object: he evokes a destiny, a sentence to be endured.
H1375.origine: The Hebrew word גָּבִיעַ (gabia) comes from a root that evokes the idea of a dome or hollow — the original meaning is that of a rounded and hollow vessel. In ancient Aramaic, words of the same family also designated cups and vases. The word appears in a context that mixes practical use (table cups) and ornamental or liturgical use (the cups of the golden candlestick).
H1375.emploi: This word appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the Pentateuch and the Prophets. In Genesis 44, it refers to Joseph's silver cup, a valuable object that becomes the center of a narrative of trial and revelation: it is by discovering the cup in Benjamin's sack that Joseph's hidden identity is revealed. In Exodus 25 and 37, the same word describes the ornaments of the sanctuary's candlestick, purely decorative and symbolic elements carved in gold. The word thus carries both the weight of a daily material object and that of a theological burden, depending on the context.
H1375.portee: Joseph's cup reminds us that God can use simple objects of life — a vessel, a possession — to test faith and reveal hidden hearts. The cups of the candlestick show us how even the ornaments of the holy place breathe order, beauty, and divine grace. These images invite the believer to see God's hand at work in the details, big or small, of His story.

sens: One who exercises authority over a group
One who dominates, who is established as a leader
H1376.detail:
1. The master is one who exercises authority and domination over others. This can refer to a superior, a lord, or a chief to whom one obeys. This is what Isaac declares to Jacob: "I have made him your master" (Genesis 27:37), acknowledging that Jacob will have authority over his brothers.
2. This term also evokes the idea of domination and power — one before whom others bow down or submit. When Isaac blesses Jacob, he announces: "May peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you!" (Genesis 27:29), showing that the master is one whose superiority is recognized through submission and obedience.
H1376.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of strength and authority. It belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words expressing power and command. The word depicts one who has the strength to lead and command, hence its meaning of "master" or "lord."
H1376.emploi: This word appears twice in Genesis, both in Genesis 27, during Isaac's blessing on Jacob. In this decisive context for the patriarchs' history, Isaac establishes Jacob not only as the heir of the promise but also as master and chief to whom his brothers — including Esau — will be subject. This term thus emphasizes the transfer of authority and the position of primacy that Jacob receives through paternal blessing.
H1376.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the importance of authority and power in the order that God establishes. Isaac's blessing on Jacob shows how God elevates and exalts certain individuals according to His plan, giving some a place of leadership and responsibility. This invites the believer to respect established authorities and to understand that all true authority comes from God.

sens: Wife of a king, royal spouse
Mother of a reigning king, queen mother
H1377.detail:
1. The queen is the wife of the king, one who shares his throne and royal rank. She bears the title and dignity of queen, like Tahpenes, the wife of Pharaoh (1 Kings 11:19), or the one mentioned alongside the king of Judah in the threat of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 13:18). The queen receives the honors attached to her position.
2. The queen mother is the mother of the reigning king, and she also holds the official title of queen. In Judah, the queen mother held a place of great importance. King Asa removed the dignity and title of queen from his own mother Maacah because she had committed idolatry (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chronicles 15:16). This removal shows that the title of queen was a dignity that could be taken away.
H1377.origine: The Hebrew word gebîrah is constructed from the root gebar, which means "to be strong, powerful." Gebîrah thus designates the powerful woman or the wife of the powerful — it is a title of honor and authority. The word rests on the image of royal strength and power.
H1377.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the accounts of the kings of Judah and Israel. It designates either the wife of the king (1 Kings 11:19) or more often the queen mother, who played a significant political role in the monarchy of Judah. Three occurrences speak of Maacah, the mother of King Asa, and the removal of her royal dignity due to her idolatry. Another refers to the sons of the queen (2 Kings 10:13). A final one, in Jeremiah, addresses the king and queen together with a prophetic message of punishment. In all cases, the term designates a woman of high rank associated with royalty.
H1377.portee: The word queen reminds the reader that women held places of influence and responsibility in the biblical monarchy. The example of Maacah also shows that rank and dignity, even the highest, are subject to God's justice: the queen mother did not escape correction or removal when she turned to idolatry. This invites the believer not to place their esteem in earthly titles but to seek first justice and faithfulness to God.

sens: Transparent and shining precious stone
Hard and shiny material found in nature
Pure and flawless substance
H1378.detail:
1. Crystal is a transparent and shining precious stone, formed naturally. It symbolizes clarity and brilliance. In Job 28:18, crystal is listed among the most precious materials — coral, pearls — to show how wisdom is even rarer and more desirable than these treasures.
2. More broadly, the word designates any hard and shiny mineral substance, crystallized by nature in the soil or rocks. It is a material of great value, sought after and prized in antiquity.
3. Figuratively, crystal evokes purity, transparency, and flawlessness, as its regular structure and brilliance embody natural perfection.
H1378.origine: The Hebrew word גָּבִישׁ comes from a root expressing clarity and brilliance. It properly designates a crystallized mineral substance, formed by nature in a regular and transparent manner. This word reflects ancient wonder at the beauty and rarity of precious minerals discovered in the earth.
H1378.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 28:18. It is found in a passage that enumerates the greatest riches of the earthly world — gold, silver, coral, pearls, crystal — to affirm that divine wisdom infinitely surpasses them in value. The use of crystal among these treasures shows that the biblical author was familiar with and highly valued this stone.
H1378.portee: Crystal reminds the reader that even the most beautiful and rare material riches — brilliant, pure, precious — are worth nothing compared to the wisdom and knowledge of God. It is an invitation to reevaluate our priorities and to seek first spiritual treasures.

sens: Mark the boundaries of a space or property
Establish a border or a restricted area
Form the natural border or limit of a territory
H1379.detail:
1. To set a limit is to draw a line that marks where something begins or ends. In Exodus 19:12, God commands Moses to set limits around Mount Sinai: no one is to touch it, or they will be punished by death. It is a material and sacred barrier that protects what is holy.
2. This verb is also used to prohibit disturbing the boundaries that were previously set. Deuteronomy 19:14 forbids moving the neighbor's boundary stones: these are the stones that delineate the fields inherited from our ancestors, and moving them would be theft. The limit guarantees everyone's rights.
3. The word also describes the natural limit formed by a river or region. In Joshua 18:20, the Jordan forms the eastern boundary of the territory of Benjamin. In Zechariah 9:2, Damascus is called the northern border: it is the limit that separates the lands.
H1379.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of surrounding, enclosing. The word belongs to the same family as a noun that designates a physical limit or boundary. The image is that of a line drawn around something to define, protect, or possess it.
H1379.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in legal and sacred geographical texts. In Exodus 19, it concerns setting a religious limit around Sinai. In Deuteronomy 19, it pertains to the boundary stones that delineate the fields and inheritances of Israelite families: it is a matter of justice and respect for property. In Joshua 18, the verb describes the territorial limits of the tribes. In Zechariah 9, it designates geographical borders. The usage progresses from the sacred (sacred mountain) to the legal (property) to the geographical (territories).
H1379.portee: This word reminds us that God establishes orders and limits to protect what is precious: the holy place, the property of others, the territory of the people. Respecting the established limits is to honor what God and our ancestors have set. Setting a limit is also to create a space of safety.

sens: Phoenician port city near Tyre, on the Mediterranean coast of the Levant
H1380.detail: Guebal is an important coastal city of Phoenicia, located north of Tyre (modern Jebeil in Lebanon). Its name means "mountain" in Hebrew, likely referring to the hills that overlook the coastline. The Greeks called it Byblus and made it a major commercial center, renowned particularly for its cedar wood and naval activities. In Ezekiel 27:9, the city appears as a provider of skilled labor for Tyre: its elders and skilled workers came to repair ships and participate in the great Mediterranean maritime trade.
H1380.origine: The Hebrew name גְּבַל (Gebal) literally means "mountain" or "hill." This same word can also refer to hills or border regions in general. The Greek name Byblus, by which the Greeks referred to this city, gave rise to the word "Bible" in French, as this city was famous in antiquity for its trade in papyrus and written texts.
H1380.emploi: Guebal appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:9, where the prophet lists the cities and peoples that participated in the prosperous trade of Tyre before its fall. In this passage, Guebal is mentioned as a supplier of skilled workers capable of repairing Tyre's ships. This unique usage highlights the strategic importance of this Phoenician city in the ancient commercial and naval networks of the Levant.

sens: mountainous region south of the Dead Sea
territory inhabited by a people allied with the enemies of Israel
H1381.detail: 1. Guébal is a mountainous region located south of the Dead Sea, in the lands of antiquity. Its name literally means "border" or "limit," as the region marks a geographical boundary. 2. The text of the Psalms shows Guébal as a region whose people allied with the enemies of Israel: in Psalm 83:8, Guébal is mentioned alongside the Ammonites, Amalekites, and Philistines, as various peoples uniting their forces against the people of God.
H1381.origine: The word Guébal comes from a Hebrew root that means "border," "limit," or "boundary." This origin well reflects the geographical situation of this territory, which marks a boundary area in the southern region of the Promised Land and adjacent territories.
H1381.emploi: Guébal appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 83:8. This psalm lists the peoples and regions allied against Israel, forming a vast enemy coalition. Guébal is cited there among other regions known for their hostility toward Israel, indicating the extent of the conflict and the opposition faced by the people of God.

sens: inhabitant of Guébal, Phoenician city-state on the Mediterranean coast
worker or craftsman from Guébal, renowned for their skills
H1382.detail: 1. The Guibliens are the inhabitants of the city of Guébal (also called Byblos), a prosperous Phoenician port located on the coast of modern Lebanon. In Joshua 13:5, the text mentions "the land of the Guibliens" as one of the regions that the Israelites had not yet possessed at the time of conquest. 2. The term also refers to the workers and craftsmen from Guébal, renowned for their expertise in woodworking and stonework. In 1 Kings 5:18, the Guibliens work alongside the workers of Solomon and Hiram to cut and prepare the materials for the construction of the Temple: the wood from Lebanon and the foundation stones.
H1382.origine: The word Guiblien comes from the name of the city of Guébal (Hebrew: גְּבַל, gəval), which literally means "border" or "limit" in Hebrew. This small port city was one of the oldest Phoenician cities, famous since antiquity for its carpenters and woodworkers. The suffix -i adds the idea of belonging or origin: a Guiblien is therefore one who comes from Guébal.
H1382.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the plural (Guibliens). First in Joshua 13:5, where it simply names a people whose lands have not yet been conquered by Israel. Then in 1 Kings 5:18, in a very different context: these are building professionals hired to contribute to the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem under Solomon. These two usages reflect the historical reality: Guébal was a small coastal kingdom that was never truly subjugated to Israel, but with which there were commercial and diplomatic relations. The Guibliens provided wood and technical expertise for Solomon's royal project.
H1382.portee: This word reminds us that the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem was not an isolated endeavor: it was part of a network of relationships with neighboring peoples, and even "unconverted" peoples could participate in the work of God. The Guibliens, while not at the heart of the Covenant, contributed with their hands and talents to the house of the Lord.

sens: Interlacing of threads, cords, or chains in a spiral
Ornament or link formed by this interlacing
H1383.detail:
1. A tress is an interlacing of threads, cords, or twisted chains together in a spiral. The image evokes a twisting motion that creates a structure that is both solid and decorative. In the breastplate of the high priest, God commands pure gold chains "twisted in the form of cords" (Exodus 28:22), showing how gold worked into a tress becomes an ornament that is both beautiful and functional.
2. By extension, the tress refers to the ornament or link produced by this interlacing. It is an element of ornamentation of the liturgical garment: these twisted chains of the breastplate are not only practical but also magnificent, reflecting the glory and holiness of the worship rendered to God.
H1383.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of twisting, wrapping, or braiding. It describes the artisanal gesture of twisting that produces a knotted structure. The tress is therefore the finished object resulting from this meticulous twisting work, typical of the Temple's craftsmanship.
H1383.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in the same two parallel verses of the Pentateuch that describe the making of the high priest's breastplate. These two passages — Exodus 28:22 and Exodus 39:15 — recount the same event twice: first God's command, then its execution. The twisted chains of pure gold form a central part of the breastplate, the most sacred liturgical garment of Mosaic worship. The context shows that the tress is a work of artisanal precision, reserved for objects of the utmost importance.
H1383.portee: The tress reminds us that the worship rendered to God requires meticulous work and beauty, not negligence or mediocrity. These gold chains are not mere accessory details, but signs that the holiness of God demands from His people an offering of art and thought, and that divine glory shines through the perfection of human craftsmanship.

sens: one who has a hump or a deformity of the back
unable to serve as a priest according to the Mosaic law
H1384.detail:
1. A hunchback is a person whose back is deformed, curved, or protruding. The image is that of a back that protrudes abnormally, giving a hunched or bumpy silhouette. In Leviticus 21:20, this physical defect is mentioned among other infirmities that render a man unfit for the priestly function.
2. In the context of Israel's worship, being a hunchback means being excluded from the priesthood. This restriction does not reflect a moral judgment on the person but applies the rule that priests must be physically 'without blemish' to represent God's perfection in the service of the tabernacle — an image of cultic purity.
H1384.origine: The Hebrew word gib.ben comes from a root that expresses the idea of curvature or deformation. It belongs to the family of terms describing visible physical defects, used notably in the priestly laws to define who may or may not officially serve God in the temple.
H1384.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 21:20. It is found in a list of physical defects disqualifying a man for the priesthood according to the Mosaic law. This list also includes blindness, lameness, a flat nose, scabs, and other infirmities. The context shows that these are criteria of cultic purity specific to the ancient worship system.
H1384.portee: This law reminds us that, in the theocracy of Israel, the physical appearance of the priest held symbolic significance: the priest was to embody the holiness and perfection due to the service of God. Although this requirement is abrogated by the new covenant, it teaches the reader that our human imperfections never disqualify us from divine grace — unlike the old law, Christ accepts us as we are.

sens: food made from curdled and aged milk
the curd, the coagulated milk
H1385.detail:
1. Cheese is a food prepared from milk that is curdled, meaning coagulated, and then possibly aged. It is a solid and durable food, very nutritious.
2. The word can also refer to the curd itself, the milk that is coagulating, before it becomes aged cheese. Job 10:10 uses this image precisely: God formed man in the womb 'like curdled milk,' suggesting a process of transformation from a liquid substance to a solid and structured substance.
H1385.origine: The Hebrew word גְּבִינָה (gevinah) is derived from a root that evokes the idea of coagulating or hardening. It belongs to the family of words describing physical transformations of substances, particularly the transition from liquid to solid. It is a concrete and everyday term in biblical culture, where cheese was a common food.
H1385.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 10:10. Job uses it poetically to describe his formation in his mother's womb: God 'poured him like milk' and 'curdled him like cheese,' illustrating how an formless and fluid substance gradually becomes a living and structured creature. It is an image of divine transformation and shaping.
H1385.portee: This image of curdling milk to form a human being reminds the believer that he is the result of a delicate and intentional work by God. It invites contemplation with gratitude of the wonderful processes of life and recognizes that our existence is not the result of chance, but of a patient and precise divine formation.

sens: rounded peak of a mountain
high point that dominates the landscape
H1386.detail:
1. The word designates the rounded peak of a mountain, its highest part. It is the image of a mountain that rises with its bumps and peaks. In Psalm 68:16, the 'mountains with many summits' of Bashan evoke this mountainous landscape with multiple rounded peaks.
2. Figuratively, the summit represents what is elevated, eminent, that which dominates. It can evoke majesty or splendor, as it rises toward the sky. The same psalm speaks of the 'mountains with many summits' enviously, as they cannot rival the mountain that God has chosen: the summit becomes the image of what aspires to importance.
H1386.origine: The Hebrew word gavnon comes from a root that expresses the idea of 'bump' or 'protrusion' — something that rises and protrudes. This root paints the natural image of a mountain with rounded and prominent contours. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe the forms of the earth's relief.
H1386.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in Psalms 68:16 and 68:17, always in the plural: 'many summits.' It designates the multiple peaks of the mountains of Bashan, a mountainous region east of the Jordan. The context is that of an enumeration of famous mountains, and the use of the plural emphasizes the abundance and majesty of the relief. These many summits look enviously at the mountain of Zion that God has chosen, which gives the word a spiritual significance: the summits, though imposing, cannot equal the mountain chosen by the Lord.
H1386.portee: This word helps the reader understand how the Bible describes creation with its visual and concrete details: the mountains, with their rounded and numerous summits, manifest the greatness of God. But the Psalm also teaches that true greatness is not in natural majesty — even the highest peaks — but in God's choice and dwelling. This invites the believer not to be impressed by what seems eminent in the eyes of the world.

sens: city of the tribe of Benjamin, located a few kilometers northeast of Jerusalem
hill or elevated point
H1387G.detail:
1. Geba is a city of Benjamin mentioned in the lists of cities (Joshua 18:24 and Ezra 2:26), inhabited by families of Benjamites (1 Chronicles 8:6). Its military importance is notable: Jonathan achieved a decisive victory there against a Philistine outpost (1 Samuel 13:3), and it served as a strategic point near Michmash. The Hebrew word literally means 'hill' or 'height,' which corresponds to the geography of the site: a city built on a steep hill.
2. The literal meaning of the word reflects the topography: Geba indeed stood on a terrifying elevation, which explains its use as a fortified position and as a landmark in the geography of the land.
H1387G.origine: The Hebrew word גֶּ֫בַע (geba) comes from a root meaning 'hill' or 'height.' It is a simple geographical term that describes the shape of the terrain. Variations of the same concept can be found in other biblical place names: Gibeah (another spelling of the same place or a nearby location) shares the same root. The name directly reflects the topography of the site: a city established on a prominent height or hill.
H1387G.emploi: Geba appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and the lists of return from exile (Ezra, Nehemiah). The city holds particular importance during the time of Saul and David: it is the site of a battle won by Jonathan against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:3), marking a turning point in Israel's struggle against its enemies. It also appears in the lists of Levitical cities (Joshua 21:17; 1 Chronicles 6:60) and in descriptions of the return from exile. In the prophetic vision of Zechariah, Geba is mentioned as a geographical boundary of the new territory (Zechariah 14:10). It remains a major geographical and administrative reference point for Benjamin.
H1387G.portee: Geba reminds us that God uses human geographies and strategic positions to accomplish His victories. Jonathan's victory at Geba against the Philistines shows how God can grant victory to a small number against a great power (1 Samuel 13:3). It is a place where the faith and courage of a young warrior changed the course of Israel's history.

sens: City of Benjamin, located about ten kilometers northeast of Jerusalem
H1387H.detail: 1. Gibeah is a city built on a steep hill in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, not far from Jerusalem. The name literally means "hill" in Hebrew, reflecting its characteristic geographical position. It is the place where the early Church would later establish its first base, and it is also the site of serious events in the history of Israel.
H1387H.origine: The Hebrew word גֶּ֫בַע (gibeah) comes from a root meaning "hill" or "height." It is a spelling variant of גִּבְעָה (gib'ah), which is more common and also refers to a hill or height. The name simply reflects the geography of the place: a city established on a hill with steep terraces.
H1387H.emploi: Gibeah appears only once in the Segond translation with this precise spelling, in the account of Judges 20:10. The passage refers to a dramatic moment: the city of Gibeah of Benjamin was the scene of a serious crime (a violation that shocked all Israel), and the text speaks of treating it according to the infamy it committed. It is in this same city that the prophet Samuel will establish his worship and where King Saul will be born, making it a central place in the ancient history of Israel.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Benjamin, located on a steep hill a few kilometers northeast of Jerusalem
H1387I.detail: Geba is a city built on a distinct rocky height, about ten kilometers northeast of Jerusalem, in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Its name literally means "hill" in Hebrew, which well describes its dominant geographical position. It is a strategic city that plays a role in military accounts, notably when David pursues the defeated Philistines from Geba to Gezer (2 Samuel 5:25), showing its importance as a starting point or landmark in ancient military campaigns.
H1387I.origine: The Hebrew name Geba means "hill" or "height." It designates a geographical site characterized by its pronounced relief — a steep hill with natural terraces. The name is transparent: it simply describes the topography of the place. This term is distinct from Gibeon (Gibéon), although in some ancient textual traditions these two places may have been confused or referred to by variant names.
H1387I.emploi: Geba appears in the account of David's victory over the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:25). It is mentioned as a geographical starting point in a military pursuit — the defeated Philistines are chased from Geba to Gezer. This shows that Geba was a well-known locality, serving as a territorial landmark in the military geography of David's time. The city occupied a strategic position between Jerusalem and the north, on the plateau of Benjamin.

sens: Place or geographical location near Gibeah in Benjamin
Site from which an Israelite ambush was launched during the war against Benjamin
H1387J.detail: 1. Maaré-Gibeah is a location situated in Israel, in the region of Benjamin, near the city of Gibeah. The name means "the meadow of the hill" or "the plains of Gibeah" — it is a well-known geographical landmark at the time of the judges. 2. This place is mentioned as the starting point of a military ambush: the men of Israel hid there to surprise the Benjaminites during a decisive battle (Judges 20:33). It was a strategic position from which the warriors could launch an unexpected attack on the enemy.
H1387J.origine: The word Gibeah (gib'ah in Hebrew) literally means "hill" or "height." Maaré means "meadow" or "plain." Together, Maaré-Gibeah thus designates a place characterized by both a hill and an open meadow — probably the plain or meadow located near the hill of Gibeah. This geographical name combines two elements that described the landscape for the inhabitants of the time.
H1387J.emploi: Maaré-Gibeah appears only once in the provided biblical texts, in Judges 20:33, in the account of the war between the tribes of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. At this point in the conflict, Israel uses this place as an ambush position. The Israelite warriors were hidden at Maaré-Gibeah, and then, at the signal, they rushed from this place to fall upon the Benjaminites by surprise. This detail shows that Maaré-Gibeah was known as an opportune place to organize an ambush attack.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H1388.detail: Gibeah is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:49. He is the son of Sheva and the grandson of Caleb. His name literally means "hill" in Hebrew, a simple designation that may evoke a geographical feature of his region of origin.
H1388.origine: The name Gibeah (גִּבְעָה) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "hill" or "height." It is a common name in Israel, borne by several places and several people in the Old Testament. Here, it is a personal name given to a descendant of Caleb, one of the great figures of the conquest of Canaan.
H1388.emploi: Gibeah appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, in the genealogy of Caleb. This passage lists the children of Caleb and their descendants, and Gibeah is presented as the son of Sheva. He is simply a member of the genealogy of the people of Judah, with no action or event recounted about him.

sens: Natural elevation of the terrain, more or less high, formed by the relief of the ground
H1389H.detail: 1. A hill is an elevation of land, a natural height less significant than a mountain. The word simply designates the geography of the place: it is a concrete term for naming the reliefs. In Joshua 5:3, the hill of Araloth is the site chosen for the collective circumcision of the children of Israel upon their entry into the promised land — a high, visible place that marks a decisive moment.
H1389H.origine: The Hebrew word גִּבְעָה (gib'ah) comes from the root that expresses the idea of rising, of elevating. It simply designates a natural height of the terrain. It is a common and ancient word in Hebrew, without particular connotation: it just speaks of the landscape.
H1389H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond 1910 translation. It names the hill of Araloth (Gibéat-Araloth in Hebrew), the place where Joshua circumcised the children of Israel after their crossing of the Jordan. It is a geographical and narrative detail: the text emphasizes that this massive circumcision took place in one location, marking the official entry of the people into God's covenant in the conquered land.
H1389H.portee: This word shows us how the Bible anchors the foundational acts of salvation in real and precise places. The circumcision at the hill of Araloth is not a vague or merely spiritual event: it took place in a concrete location, reminding us that God acts in real history and in earthly space. This teaches us that our faith is not detached from the material world.

sens: Small mountain or elevation of land
Place of idol worship or forbidden rituals
Poetic image to designate a mountain or height in general
H1389I.detail:
1. The hill is an elevation of the ground lower than a mountain, a natural height of the terrain. It is clearly seen in action in historical accounts: it is on a hill that Israel settles or takes refuge, as David and his men did on the hill of Hachilah (1 Samuel 26:1), or as Joab pursued Abner to the hill of Amma (2 Samuel 2:24).

2. Hills are also places of worship — often illicit. Judah builds shrines and plants idols on the hills (1 Kings 14:23), and the Israelites commit spiritual adultery there (Jeremiah 13:27). It is there that pagan worship prohibited by the law of Moses took place (Deuteronomy 12:2). The prophets denounce this practice: the hills become a symbol of sin and unfaithfulness to God.

3. In poetry, the hill rises to the level of the mountain: it symbolizes elevation, strength, stability. The psalms sing of how the hills leap for joy like lambs (Psalms 114:4), and God descends to fight "on the mountain of Zion and on its hill" (Isaiah 31:4) — this majestic language elevates the hill to the rank of a symbol of the divine.
H1389I.origine: The Hebrew word גִּבְעָה (gibah) etymologically means a "bump," a rounded shape: it is imagined as an animal's back gently rising from the ground. It is a simple and natural formation, much less imposing than a mountain (har). The word appears 67 times in the Bible, mostly in the prophets and in historical narratives where the terrain plays a narrative role.
H1389I.emploi: The hill appears 67 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a concrete and narrative context. In the literal sense, it localizes places: it is from the top of a hill that Moses sees Amalek fighting (Exodus 17:9-10), it is on a hill that the Israelites achieve victory (Judges 7:1). In the spiritual sense, it becomes a place of disobedience: the kings of Israel erect shrines on the hills (2 Kings 16:4; 2 Kings 17:10), committing the idolatrous rites that the Torah forbids. This is why the prophets often reserve the hill for divine punishment: Ezekiel sees "the dead on its hills" (Ezekiel 35:8). But in prophetic poetry, the image grows: the hill becomes a symbol of eternal stability (Genesis 49:26) or of God's kingship (Isaiah 2:2).
H1389I.portee: For the Christian reader, the hill reveals how the people of God have too often sought the divine elsewhere than near Him, on the high places of disobedience. It reminds us of the danger of following the practices of the world around us. But it also speaks of God's stability, capable of transforming heights into places of His victory and peace.

sens: Mountain town in Judah
H1390G.detail: Gibeah is a small town located in the mountainous region of Judah. Its Hebrew name literally means "hill," reflecting its elevated geographical position. It is mentioned in the list of cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:57).
H1390G.origine: The name Gibeah comes directly from the Hebrew word giv'ah, which means "hill" or "small height." It is a descriptive name that simply designates the topography of the place. Several locations in Israel bear this name or a related name, as hills were important geographical landmarks in the mountainous landscape of Judah.
H1390G.emploi: Gibeah is attested twice in the Old Testament. It first appears in the list of cities belonging to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:57), listed among other localities in the mountainous region. It is then mentioned in 2 Chronicles 13:2 as the birthplace of Micajah, mother of King Abijah. It is a secondary locality of the kingdom of Judah, without a specific narrative dedicated to it.

sens: city of the tribe of Benjamin, located on a hill
birthplace and residence of King Saul
center of an abominable crime reported in the book of Judges
theater of a bloody battle between Benjamin and the other tribes
H1390H.detail:
1. Gibeah is a fortified city of Benjamin, built on a height (the Hebrew name literally means "hill"). It is mentioned about 42 times in the Bible, primarily in the historical accounts of the Old Testament.
2. Gibeah is especially famous as the birthplace and residence of King Saul, the first king of Israel. It is there that Samuel comes to seek Saul, and it is from this city that he establishes his power (1 Samuel 13:15; 1 Samuel 10:5).
3. Gibeah is the scene of a horrific sexual crime: a Levite and his concubine are welcomed there at night, but men of the city rape and kill the woman. This outrage provokes a revolt of Israel against Benjamin (Judges 20:5).
4. The city becomes the center of a bloody civil war: after the crime, the tribes of Israel rise up against Benjamin. The sons of Benjamin come out of Gibeah to fight, but after three days of battle, Benjamin is crushed, leaving thousands dead on the ground (Judges 20:21, 20:37).
H1390H.origine: The Hebrew name גִּבְעָה (giv'ah) comes from a root meaning "to elevate" or "to stand up"; it literally designates a hill or height. It is a descriptive geographical name: Gibeah is thus named because it is built at altitude, making it visible and easily fortifiable. The name also appears in compounds like "Gibeath-Phinehas" (the hill of Phinehas) in Joshua 24:33.
H1390H.emploi: Gibeah appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mostly in 1 Samuel and in the book of Judges. It is first the scene of a crime that shocks and divides Israel (Judges 19-20); this account is recalled by the prophets Hosea and Isaiah as an example of moral perversion (Hosea 5:8, 9:9; Isaiah 10:29). Then, it becomes the heart of Saul's political power: it is from Gibeah that he governs the beginnings of the kingdom (1 Samuel 13:15, 14:2, 15:34), and it is at Gibeah that the king and his warriors gather. The city also symbolizes defeat and shame: in 2 Samuel 21:6, the Gibeonites ask that seven descendants of Saul be hanged "before the Lord at Gibeah."
H1390H.portee: Gibeah reminds the reader that sexual sin and violence provoke terrible judgments, even within the people of God (the crime of Judges 19-20 leads to the near-extinction of Benjamin). It also shows that political power, even established by God through Saul, can be marked by selfishness and injustice. As the first capital of the kingdom, Gibeah teaches us that true kingship is not in the fortifications of a city, but in obedience to God.

sens: Fortified city of the tribe of Benjamin, located about 8 km from Jerusalem
H1391.detail: Gibeon was an important city in the territory of Benjamin, inhabited by the Hivites (descendants of Canaan). It was located near Jerusalem. The inhabitants of Gibeon made a peace treaty with Joshua and the Israelites (Joshua 9:3), which saved their lives while other Canaanite cities were conquered. After the conquest, Gibeon became a Levitical city (Joshua 21:17) and an important religious center: it was there that the tabernacle and the high place of worship were located, where Solomon received a divine vision (1 Kings 3:5).
H1391.origine: The name means "the city of the hill" or "the hill" in Hebrew. The archaeological site, identified as el-Jib, confirms its strategic importance as a high urban center in the hills of the land of Benjamin. Gibeon played a crucial role in the history of Israel from the conquest of the land.
H1391.emploi: Gibeon appears 36 times in the Bible, mainly in the books of the Old Testament recounting the conquest (Joshua), the history of the kings (1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles), and prophetic testimonies (Jeremiah, Isaiah). It is the scene of several major events: the negotiation of the peace treaty during the conquest (Joshua 9), the great battle against the Amorite kings (Joshua 10:5), battles between David's troops and those of Ish-Bosheth (2 Samuel 2:16), and the stay of the tabernacle under David (1 Chronicles 16:39). It is also the place where God appeared to Solomon in a dream (1 Kings 3:5). Gibeon thus symbolizes cunning (the negotiated treaty), divine victory, and the centrality of worship in Israel.
H1391.portee: Gibeon reminds us that God can grant unexpected grace to those who humbly ask for it, even during a military conquest. The presence of the tabernacle in Gibeon for decades shows that the worship of the true God was established in the land according to divine plans. It is also a place where God miraculously manifested Himself and listened to the prayers of the kings of Israel.

sens: Stage of the plant where flowers or floral buds appear
Moment when the plant prepares to produce its seeds
H1392.detail: 1. Blossoming is the moment when a plant produces its flowers or floral buds: it is the stage where the plant is preparing to reproduce. In Exodus 9:31, the flax was in bloom at the time of the hail plague, which means that the flowers or reproductive organs of the flax were formed and visible, making the harvest vulnerable to destruction. 2. This term also broadly refers to the moment when the plant concentrates its forces on reproductive production, before the formation of seeds. It is a key period in the growth cycle: once this stage is reached, the plant has invested significantly, and a sudden destruction (like hail) compromises the entire harvest.
H1392.origine: The Hebrew word giv'ol comes from a root that denotes what blooms or flourishes. It is related to the image of the plant unfolding and opening to produce its flowers. The agricultural context of Exodus shows that this word particularly applies to crops that produce seeds, such as flax and barley.
H1392.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 9:31, in the account of the seventh plague of Egypt (the hail). It is used to describe the state of the flax at the moment when God sends the hail: the flax was precisely in bloom, while the barley was already in ears (more advanced). This difference in growth stage explains why only certain crops were struck: the hail occurs at a critical moment when the flax, in full bloom, cannot withstand it, illustrating the precision of the divine plague and the impotence of the Egyptian gods.
H1392.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of crops and human plans in the face of God's action. The destruction of the flax in bloom shows that God does not strike randomly, but at the moment when the blow will be most devastating. This invites the believer to recognize divine sovereignty over nature and events, even the most destructive ones.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Gibeon
Member of a non-Israelite population allied to Israel by treaty
Indigenous people of the Amorites whose descendants survived
Person bound to Israel by sacred oath
H1393.detail: 1. The Gibeonites are the inhabitants of Gibeon, a city in Canaan located in the mountainous region (the name means "little hill"). Gibeon was an important and fortified settlement, not just a simple village. 2. This people is not of Israelite origin: they are survivors of the Amorites, the indigenous peoples that the Israelites conquered upon entering Canaan (2 Samuel 21:2). 3. The Gibeonites obtained a peace treaty with Joshua and the Israelites by cunning: they pretended to come from very far away so that the Israelites would spare them, and a solemn oath bound them (the text of Joshua explains this story). 4. This oath had the force of sacred law, which could not be broken without serious consequences: when Saul massacred Gibeonites out of zeal for Israel, a famine struck the land until David brought justice to the survivors (2 Samuel 21:1-9).
H1393.origine: The Hebrew word comes from Gibeon (גִּבְעוֹן), the name of their city. Gibeon means "hill" or "little hill" — a geographical name that designates both the place and its inhabitants. In the Old Testament, Gibeon, the strategic city of Benjamin, is often distinguished from Gibeon "the great" (another nearby settlement). The name recalls the mountainous and hilly terrain of the Benjamin plateau.
H1393.emploi: The Gibeonites mainly appear in the history of David during the time of famine (2 Samuel 21). Several uses show how this non-Israelite people was integrated into the people of God by sacred treaty. Saul violated this commitment by persecuting them, which provoked the Lord's wrath. David, recognizing its legitimacy, asks them for reparation and executes their sentence against the sons of Saul. A Gibeonite is also found among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 12:4), showing that some Gibeonites had integrated into the royal army. The term thus designates both a distinct group and an element of the people of Israel united by covenant.
H1393.portee: The story of the Gibeonites teaches that oaths and alliances, even those made by cunning at the outset, are sacred before God and cannot be violated without consequences. It also shows that non-Israelites who enter into alliance with the people of God receive His protection and blessings. Finally, it reveals how a promise made to enemies becomes a moral obligation that just kings must honor, even at the cost of painful sacrifice.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin
H1394.detail: Gibeah is a city belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the territorial inheritance that this tribe received during the division of the promised land among the Israelites. It appears in the list of fourteen cities and villages assigned to Benjamin (Joshua 18:28).
H1394.origine: The name Gibeah comes from the Hebrew גִּבְעָה (giv'ah), which literally means "hill" or "height." This word describes a city situated on elevated ground, characteristic of the localities of Judea. Another spelling of the same name appears elsewhere in the Bible, but all designate fortified places or remarkable for their geographical position.
H1394.emploi: Gibeah appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 18:28, in the context of the drawing of lots for the lands among the tribes of Israel. It is mentioned as one of the cities that the tribe of Benjamin received as an inheritance after the conquest of Canaan. This enumeration is part of the process by which God distributes the promised territory according to the twelve tribes.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Gibeah
H1395.detail: 1. The word designates a person from Gibeah, the city of Benjamin. In the passage where it appears (1 Chronicles 12:3), Jehu is identified as "from Gibeah" (or "Gibeahite"), which means he comes from this city and bears its name of origin.
H1395.origine: The word comes from Gibeah (גִּבְעָה in Hebrew), which literally means "hill" or "height." It is a city in the territory of Benjamin, already mentioned in the Old Testament as an important place in the Israelite monarchy. The Hebrew suffix indicates belonging: one who is from Gibeah.
H1395.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible (1 Chronicles 12:3), where it applies to Jehu, one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag. In this context, the geographical indication "from Gibeah" served to clearly identify where this warrior came from among David's ranks.

sens: Increase in volume or intensity
Be strong, powerful, capable
Triumph, overcome by strength
Dominate, show greater strength than
Be courageous, act vigorously
Act with pride or insolence toward God
H1396.detail:
1. Increase in volume or intensity: the word first describes a physical phenomenon — the water that "grows," meaning it rises and spreads. During the flood, the waters "grew" and increased on the earth (Genesis 7:18), and they "were strong" for one hundred fifty days (Genesis 7:24).
2. Be strong, powerful, capable: the word designates strength itself, capacity, power. Judah was "mighty" among his brothers (1 Chronicles 5:2). It is the quality of one who has vigor, physically or morally.
3. Triumph, overcome by strength: "man shall not prevail by strength" (1 Samuel 2:9) — this means not winning the victory. The word evokes the idea of carrying away, surpassing the opponent in battle.
4. Dominate, show greater strength than: to have superiority. When Moses lifts his hand, Israel prevails; when he lowers it, Amalek prevails (Exodus 17:11).
5. Be courageous, act vigorously: it is also to show boldness and determination. The goodness of God is "great" (Psalms 103:11) — the same word means that it surpasses, that it excels.
6. Act with pride or insolence toward God: the word can also describe guilty pride. In Job 36:9, we speak of man's pride — a strength turned toward oneself rather than toward good.
H1396.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּבַר (gabar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of growing, becoming great or intense. It belongs to the family of words designating strength, greatness, and power. The base form (Qal) describes the state of being strong or prevailing; the other forms (Piel, Hiphil, Hithpael) allow for expressing the action of making strong, fortifying, or showing oneself proudly. This word reflects the image of a strength that grows, imposes itself, dominates.
H1396.emploi: The verb gabar appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, psalms, and wisdom literature. In the concrete sense, it describes a physical increase, such as that of the floodwaters (Genesis 7:18, 7:24). In the figurative sense, it expresses the strength of a nation (Judah "mighty" in 1 Chronicles 5:2), success in battle (Exodus 17:11, where Israel "prevails"), or moral excellence (the goodness of God in Psalms 103:11). The reflexive form (Hithpael) appears to express guilty pride — acting presumptuously before God (Job 36:9, Job 15:25). The word thus nuances from the more objective (having strength) to the more moral (using one's strength correctly or not).
H1396.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on true strength: not domination through brutality, but just power submitted to God. When Moses lifts his hands in prayer, Israel "prevails" — it is a lesson on the power of intercession and trust in God rather than in weapons. The word also warns us of the danger of pride: acting "strongly" against God is foolish. It reminds us that only God's strength is enduring.

sens: human male, as opposed to woman
adult man in full strength
warrior, fighter
remarkable character, man of value
human creature before God
H1397.detail:
1. The word designates a human male: it is man in his gender condition. In Exodus 10:11, Pharaoh asks for "the men" to serve the Lord, implicitly distinguishing them from women and children.

2. It refers to a man in the prime of life, capable of acting and deciding. In 1 Chronicles 23:3, the Levites are counted "by man" from thirty years old: this is the age when a man has vigor and experience.

3. The word often emphasizes the capacity to fight. In Numbers 24:3 and 24:15, Balaam is described as "the man with the open eye," meaning the warrior prophet or wise one in the strength of his means.

4. It is also the remarkable man, one who stands out for his qualities or destiny. In Job 34:7, it is said, "Is there a man like Job?", admiring his wisdom and resilience.

5. Finally, it is the human creature in its fragility before God. In Psalms 89:49, one wonders, "Is there a man who can live and not see death?", expressing the mortality of every man before the eternal.
H1397.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses strength and capacity for action: the basic idea is that of virility, power, and the ability to fulfill a role. In Hebrew, it contrasts with "woman" (אִשָּׁה, ishah) and "child" (יֶלֶד, yeled). Its use in the Psalms and Job also shows that this term acquires an existential dimension: man aware of his mortality and his relationship with God.
H1397.emploi: The word appears about 64 times in the Old Testament, very often in the poetic books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and narrative books (Jeremiah, Chronicles). In Exodus, Numbers, and Joshua, it is often used to count or designate fighters. In the Psalms and Job, it takes on an existential significance: man facing death, God, his destiny. In Proverbs, it often characterizes the wise man or the strong man, capable of mastering his passions (Proverbs 24:5: "A wise man is better than a thousand warriors"). Jeremiah uses it to speak of man's fragility before God's judgments (Jeremiah 17:5: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man").
H1397.portee: This word reminds the reader that man possesses strength, capacity for action, and responsibility — but he is also fundamentally mortal and fragile before God. That is why the Bible emphasizes both the dignity of man created in the image of God and his helplessness without God. For the believer, this word invites placing trust not in human strength, but in God alone.

sens: Officer of King Solomon, son of Uri
H1398.detail: Gever is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is an officer in the service of King Solomon, son of Uri, responsible for administering the region of Gilead east of the Jordan. He oversees the territories formerly conquered by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, which shows the extent of his authority under Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:19).
H1398.origine: The name Gever means "warrior" or "mighty man" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes virile strength and courage. Such names were borne by great figures or military and civil leaders of the royal period in Israel.
H1398.emploi: Gever appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:19. He is listed among the twelve officers that Solomon had established over Israel to provide for the maintenance of his royal household. Each was in charge of a region. Gever governs Gilead and the lands east of the Jordan, highlighting the importance of his role in the administration of the unified kingdom.

sens: male person
individual endowed with strength and ability
upright man, of moral value
H1399.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man, a male person, in contrast to a woman. It is the general term for speaking of a male individual in all his concrete reality.
2. It also carries the idea of a strong, capable man, someone who possesses vigor and maturity — a man in the fullest sense of the term, with his strength of character and responsibility.
3. In certain contexts, it specifically applies to the good man, one who acts with righteousness and moral integrity. This is how it appears in Psalms 18:26, where David states: "With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the upright man you show yourself upright" — here, "the man" is one who walks in justice and faithfulness toward God.
H1399.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of strength and virility. It is very close to the classical word גֶּ֫בֶר (gever), which emphasizes this notion of a strong, virile, warrior man. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to power and ability. It is a fundamental term for speaking of man in his dimension as a responsible and active person.
H1399.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond in Psalms 18:26. It specifically designates the upright man, one whose conduct is just and loyal toward God. In this verse, David presents a principle of divine governance: God shows himself good to the one who is good, just to the one who acts uprightly. The usage emphasizes that God responds to each according to his heart and way of life. It is an implicit call to be that "upright man" to whom God will grant his favor.
H1399.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the term "man" is not neutral: the Bible values the upright man, one who walks in integrity and justice. This confronts us with the question: what kind of man am I? Am I one who acts with righteousness toward God and others? The entry invites us to see that our moral integrity shapes our relationship with God himself.
